data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Burnham’s devolution drive to cost bus operator £260m
data.description:
One of Britain’s biggest bus operators stands to lose £260m from Andy Burnham’s move to hand increased powers to local mayors.

FirstGroup, which runs routes across the UK, said the figure represented lost revenue from services it operates in Wales and Yorkshire that are set to come under municipal control as part of the Prime Minister’s local transport crusade.

The UK is set to move away from privatisation to a bus franchising model whereby local authorities take over fleets and depots and then hire firms to operate them.

Graham Sutherland, FirstGroup’s chief executive, said a franchising model set to be rolled out would deliver lower margins, prompting the group to invest in more dependable markets such as coaches and London buses.

FirstGroup’s switch away from the regions highlights the risks of the Prime Minister’s decision to place buses at the heart of his devolution drive.

It was revealed in August that the West Midlands had been hit with a £30m bill after National Express chose to exit local buses completely in response to franchising, forcing the combined authority to buy out 1,400 vehicles and a network of depots.

FirstGroup’s renewed focus on London comes after it quit the capital in 2013 amid a clampdown by Transport for London (TfL) on the value of contracts.

It reversed the move in December 2024 – less than six months after Labour came to power – with the £90m takeover of RATP London, followed last year by the purchase of the Tootbus sightseeing fleet.

The firm now has more than 1,000 buses in London, with revenue this year expected to rise to £350m, an increase of 13pc.

Mr Sutherland said the franchising of buses in West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire and Wales would deprive FirstGroup of around 30pc of its £890m a year in regional bus revenue.

Industry-wide, he said firms faced a slump of £1.5bn a year in revenue in regions that had already announced their intention to move to franchising.

“We will have materially less regional buses in operation. We’ve diversified on the basis that these policy changes were going to impact our regional bus business,” he said.

“We’re still confident that over the next period of tranches we can continue to grow our bus business.”

FirstGroup said it would monitor plans announced by Lord Khan of Tooting for a new public company – Buses for London – which would compete in the capital, where a franchising model already operates but private firms are allowed to operate their own bus fleets and depots.

Mr Sutherland said: “It’s a handful of routes and a small part of the London network at this point. We don’t think it changes much in the short term and we’re confident that the costs and value we provide will stand up in comparison against any operator.”

Industry sources have called the proposals “mad” and “a Sadiq Khan vanity project” that would heap costs on TfL, which is £14bn in debt.

data.title: Burnham accused of dodging scrutiny after ditching press pack
data.description:
Andy Burnham has been accused of avoiding media scrutiny for not taking a full press contingent to two international conferences.

In an unusual move, the Prime Minister chose not to take the normal “press pack” to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, or to Cop31 in Turkey on Thursday.

Guto Harri, the former No 10 director of communications for Boris Johnson, said he had seen travelling to CHOGM with the pack as “loading the plane with a bunch of assassins determined to take out the PM I worked for, but that’s the deal”.

At the last CHOGM in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer took a full press contingent nearly 10,000 miles across the world to Samoa, and held both a press conference and an on-the-record grilling by journalists on the government plane.

Mr Harri said: “You sign up for scrutiny. You agree to be accountable. It’s at the heart of our democracy, and for someone as articulate as Andy Burnham to avoid the press on such an important occasion is not only a sign of weakness but concern.

“I appreciate he does a lot of communication, he does quite a lot of decent interviews, but his modus operandi seems increasingly to be to provide reasons for not answering, not to mention, more importantly, addressing the big questions that a leader needs to tackle, and that’s the one to watch.”

A government source said Mr Burnham had taken part in two pool interviews on Thursday, one in Turkey for COP31 and one in Dublin, as well as a huddle in Dublin where the Prime Minister took 16 questions, including one from The Telegraph.

CHOGM ended up dominating headlines, as the Prime Minister became embroiled in diplomatic clashes over the Commonwealth’s future relevance and slavery reparations.

It is not the first time Mr Burnham has appeared to avoid the press.

In June, the morning after Mr Burnham’s Makerfield by-election victory, he rallied supporters at Ashton Town football club’s ground but did not take questions from the press, nor did he at his scene-setting speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester just over a week later.

The day he took office, Mr Burnham managed just four questions in seven minutes in an informal, unfilmed huddle with political editors in Downing Street’s Rose Garden before being ushered away for his first call with Donald Trump.

No 10 said it would rearrange the event, but did not, The Telegraph understands.

Government sources said Mr Burnham’s huddle on the first day showed that the Prime Minister’s first instinct was to speak to lobby journalists.

In a similar way to his predecessors, Mr Burnham was interviewed by broadcasters in the run-up to the Labour Party conference in September.

In an interview with ITV at the start of the month, he was asked whether he cared less than his predecessors about what the traditional media said about him. Mr Burnham replied: “Oh, definitely. Well, you see, I left Westminster for a reason.

“I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there, and then the whole world meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that any more.”

Mr Burnham has been interviewed by TikTok and Instagram influencers. However, critics said he was “running away from being asked questions” by traditional journalists by choosing his own interviewers on social media.

Two weeks before he entered No 10, the future Prime Minister took to Reddit for an “Ask Me Anything” session, inviting users to send in their questions.

However, Mr Burnham chose to avoid queries on why the Government was “unable to do major infrastructure projects in this country” or whether he had plans to unfreeze income tax thresholds.

One Reddit user, after his question on “scandalous” student loans was left unanswered, wrote: “Oh Andy, you bottled it. At least we know what the next prime minister’s favourite films are I suppose.”

After his first Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs), Mr Burnham took to answering social media questions for “People’s Major Questions”, which he called “the real PMQs”.

At the time, Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, told journalists: “I don’t need to use Reddit because I’m happy to take questions from the media.

“Andy Burnham, I’m amazed, was running away from being asked questions. Reddit is easy.”

Matt Vickers, the deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, told The Telegraph: “As mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham never met a camera he didn’t like. Now he’s Prime Minister, he’s gone into hiding.

“The Prime Minister has questions to answer about the tax rises and broken promises piling up on his watch. Social media skits are no substitute for serious scrutiny.

“If he cannot face a room of journalists, how on earth can he face the country?”

Industry sources also warned against the Government’s increasing use of so-called “vanity photographers”, who are employed by No 10 and instructed to take carefully staged photographs of politicians.

Sources told The Telegraph that greater use of internal photographers meant the public only saw a glimpse into the side of politics the Government wanted them to see, in contrast to the images typically taken by the traditional news media.

Some of the most widely distributed photographs surrounding the Budget were taken by No 10 PR photographers, including a prominently used photograph of John Healey’s selfie with his Treasury team.

Sir John Whittingdale, the chairman of the all-party parliamentary group on media freedom, told The Telegraph: “At a time of growing disinformation and social media influence, it is even more important to support professional journalism and mainstream media who can properly hold government to account.

“Access to the Prime Minister is an essential part of that and I hope Andy Burnham will follow the example of his predecessors in regularly making himself available.”

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: TG Jones scrambles to avoid being the high street’s next victim
data.description:
When private equity firm Modella Capital snapped up the 464 branches of WH Smith last year, it promised a bright future.

Modella bosses claimed their skills and expertise would “unlock sustainable growth and re-establish these stores as the hub of high streets they serve”.

It did not turn out that way. Little more than a year after inking the £40m deal, the new owners’ legal team was in the High Court arguing the case for a radical restructuring to avert imminent insolvency of a business rebadged as TG Jones.

Less than four months after Mr Justice Hildyard approved that overhaul, Modella appears to have had enough of the troublesome chain.

Modella said on Tuesday it had received “unsolicited offers” for TG Jones, prompting it to appoint corporate adviser Teneo – a firm best known for its insolvency work – to “review” the proposals from the potential suitors.

Some in the industry believe the Modella top brass, led by Joe Price, the managing director and co-founder, have been spooked by the political furore that has engulfed fellow high street struggler Poundland and its owners Gordon Brothers, and are now keen to offload TG Jones.

As one observer put it: “Modella realised they could be in exactly the same place in a few months’ time.”

Modella insiders dismiss this suggestion, insisting that the timing of Teneo’s appointment was entirely driven by the unexpected approaches.

Whatever the truth of the matter, the appointment has raised the question: can TG Jones ever be a success?

In the year after the rebranding, sales at the already struggling high street chain slumped by a further 12pc as consumers shunned the obviously underinvested-in stores and the cheap and not particularly cheerful fascia tacked on to their frontages.

The deterioration in trading was so dramatic that a radical restructuring became inevitable to avoid TG Jones running dry of cash “in very short order indeed”, as Mr Justice Hildyard put it.

The rescue involved the closure of 150 of the company’s worst-performing stores, as well as rent cuts and freezes, reduced payments to “non-core suppliers” and a £15m cash injection from Modella.

The sad process of shutting the unsaveable stores – some that stood as WH Smith branches for decades – continues remorselessly, leaving ugly new gaps in high streets already pockmarked by closures.

Over the coming months dozens more will shut, many dragging Post Offices with them to the retail graveyard.

Branches scheduled for the knacker’s yard over the coming weeks and currently shrouded in yellow “everything must go” closing-down banners include those in Brighton, Hungerford, Peterborough, Falmouth, Dover and Dundee.

Each shuttering is a blow for the communities those stores have served. The closure in Brighton will leave shoppers in its city centre without access to postal services for the first time since 1750.

It is all a far cry from the optimistic early days last spring. Modella chiefs hoped to build a new high street force offering a remarkably diverse range of products and services, from Isas to Airfix model kits.

The existing relationship with Post Offices and Toys R Us would carry on, and other Modella investments such as Hobbycraft and Claire’s would open concessions.

Sean Toal, the then chief executive, promised landlords at a conference in November last year that footfall would be fuelled by “multiple missions – read through books, use the magazines, learn through our stationery range, play with our Toys R Us ranges, and post and bank”.

However, Catherine Shuttleworth, the founder of the Savvy Marketing agency, says TG Jones has struggled to stand out in a crowded marketplace.

“In every category they are in, someone else does it better and cheaper, whether it’s B&M, the supermarkets or sweet shops.

“I was in the Woodbridge branch the other day and it was the ‘back to school’ time of year. But they couldn’t convince me to buy a single thing. The offer just wasn’t compelling enough and the pricing wasn’t sharp enough. I could get all the back to school stuff cheaper at Tesco.”

The rebrand was also costly. When WH Smith put its high street branches up for sale last year to focus on its travel outlets, the illustrious brand was not part of the deal. That forced a rebrand.

When it revealed the made-up name of TG Jones, Modella insisted it “carries the same sense of family and reflects these stores being at the heart of everyone’s high street”.

But the change of ownership – and identity – did not land well with the British shopping public already less than enthused by WH Smith’s tired offering of books, sweets and stationery.

Insiders at TG Jones, now led by Alex Willson, insist the restructuring and a welcome stabilisation in trading have lifted the immediate threat of insolvency. “There’s a feeling it’s got a future,” said one.

But the Poundland debacle inevitably casts a dark shadow over a sector that has seen some of its most notorious collapses happen in the run-up to Christmas, notably Woolworths in November 2008 and Debenhams in December 2020.

The timing of Teneo’s appointment is scarcely helpful. As Richard Hyman, a veteran retail watcher, puts it: “By confirming this surely they have unsettled senior management, staff suppliers and customers. Where on earth is the rationale for that? I’m a bit mystified.”

Jittery suppliers were already unnerved by the terms of the aggressive restructuring, which left some having to shoulder heavy write-offs. Others, including big names such as Condé Nast, the magazine publisher, Ferrero, the chocolate manufacturer, and Lonely Planet, the guidebook group, were forced to accept lengthy delays in payment.

One insolvency specialist, Molly Monks, the founder of the corporate recovery firm Parker Walsh, ominously advised suppliers “that a familiar brand name and a long-standing commercial relationship are no guarantee of financial protection”.

It is not an encouraging backdrop to the auction of a business that stayed in the same hands for more than two centuries, but now faces a second disruptive change of control in less than two years.

Who could be running the rule over TG Jones?

Those falling squarely in the category of “usual suspects” include those known to have been sniffing around the business when it was still owned by WH Smith.

Prominent names in the frame are rescue specialists Hilco Capital, which has previously owned brands including HMV, Cath Kidston, and Homebase, as well as Alteri Investors, which has fashion brand Austin Reed and kitchen supplier Magnet in its stable.

Others suggest that TG Jones may be beyond saving in its current form, and that the estate will be broken up and swallowed by supermarkets looking to boost their town centre presence.

After the WH Smith brand spent more than 230 years as a fixture of our high streets, there are fears its successor may not last much more than a year.

data.title: Nine steps to protect your money from a cyber attack
data.description:
From high street shops and online marketplaces to supermarket fridges, hackers have exposed how fragile our companies and systems are in a wide-ranging wave of recent cyber attacks.

While much of this is out of your control, you can at least take action to protect your money and personal information – and you don’t have to be particularly tech-savvy to do it.

Kiran Fothergill, of Sapphire Security Services, explained: “Think of it like securing your home. You wouldn’t leave your front door unlocked, hand your keys to a stranger or ignore a broken window. The same common sense should apply online.”

We’ve spoken to cyber security experts to explain the simple steps you can take today to make yourself a harder target for criminals.

1. Lock down your most important accounts

One of the first steps you should take is ensuring your most important accounts are secure.

Zain Javed, of cyber security platform Citation Cyber, said: “If you only make one change today, turn on two-factor authentication, particularly for your email, banking and social media accounts.

“This adds an extra layer of security, so even if a criminal steals your password, they will usually need another form of verification to access your account.”

With two-factor authentication, you’ll usually be asked for a second proof of identity when you sign in, such as a code sent to your phone or generated by an authenticator app.

Free authenticator apps include Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Google Authenticator. Where available, using an app rather than receiving codes by text message is generally more secure, as text messages can be intercepted or diverted.

2. Don’t reuse passwords

Remembering umpteen different passwords across various websites isn’t easy. But resist the temptation to use the same password across multiple sites.

Doing so means that if one website has a data breach, criminals could try using your stolen login details to access your other accounts.

Instead, you could use a password manager, such as 1Password or Bitwarden, to generate and securely store unique passwords for different accounts.

Jonathan Lee, of cybersecurity platform TrendAI, said: “Pay particular attention to your personal email account. It can be the front door to much of your digital life, because access to your email may allow someone to reset passwords for other critical services you rely on.”

If passkeys are available on websites, these can be even better than traditional passwords. They let you sign in using your fingerprint, facial recognition or your screen lock PIN.

3. Protect your identity

Your personal information is valuable to criminals, so it’s worth taking steps to protect it.

Mr Fothergill said: “Identity protection services can help you monitor your personal information and identify potential exposure or suspicious activity.

“They aren’t a guarantee against identity theft, but they can provide an additional early warning and help you respond more quickly.”

However, you might not need to pay for a specialist service.

Paul Bischoff, of research company Comparitech, said: “Identity protection apps don’t do much that you can’t do yourself, such as monitoring bank accounts and credit. For most of us, these apps are mainly a convenience.”

Instead, you can take some simple steps such as regularly checking your bank and credit card statements for unfamiliar transactions, checking your free credit report for accounts you don’t recognise, and being alert to unexpected password reset emails.

4. Don’t give personal details to AI

With increasing numbers of people turning to AI to ask for advice on everything from medical issues to personal finance, you need to think carefully about the information you share.

Tom Vazdar, of Open Institute of Technology, said: “Treat an AI chatbot like a stranger with a very good memory. Conversations may be stored, read by reviewers or leaked. Don’t type in passwords, bank details, ID documents, medical records or work files.”

Also check your provider’s privacy settings as not all AI platforms handle data in the same way.

Charles Radclyffe, of EA Global AI, said: “Consumer AI tools may use user interactions to help improve and train their models, so users should think carefully before sharing personal information.”

5. Don’t ignore app and device updates

Another simple but important step is to ensure you have turned on automatic updates on your phone, laptop, web browser and apps. It can pay to keep the built-in security features on your devices switched on, too.

Mr Javed said: “Those software update notifications we all put off are actually one of the simplest ways to protect ourselves.

“Cybercriminals regularly exploit known weaknesses in outdated software. Manufacturers release updates to fix these vulnerabilities, but those fixes only protect you once they’re installed.”

6. Guard your bank account

Scammers are finding ever more convincing ways to part people from their cash, which makes it even more important to be on your guard.

Mr Javed said: “The days of spotting a scam because of poor spelling or bad grammar are disappearing. AI means criminals can now write convincing messages and even imitate familiar voices.”

To protect yourself, agree a family code word and ask for it if someone calls asking for money.

Mr Fothergill added: “Criminals are very good at creating a sense of urgency. You might receive a text claiming there’s suspicious activity on your bank account or a telephone call warning that your money is at risk. The golden rule is never to act under pressure.”

This means never clicking on links in unexpected messages or sharing passwords, Pins or security codes with someone who contacts you. If you’re unsure, always hang up and contact your bank directly using the number on the website or through the official app.

Remember, your bank will never ask for your Pin or account details or request you transfer money into a so-called “safe account”.

7. Stick to familiar websites

When shopping online, stick to trusted websites you’ve used before. Criminals can create convincing copies of genuine websites, so check the web address carefully before entering any personal or payment details.

Even if the website has a padlock symbol or “https” address, this doesn’t mean the website is safe.

You should also be wary of adverts and offers that seem too good to be true.

Jamie Akhtar, of cybersecurity platform CyberSmart, said: “Cybercriminals are quick to exploit trending topics, using the excitement surrounding popular games, new film releases and other cultural moments to trick unsuspecting users into clicking malicious links or downloading harmful content.

“If you receive a message promising exclusive access, early releases or special offers, take a moment to verify that it comes from a legitimate source before clicking any links or sharing personal information.”

8. Delete apps you don’t use

Most of us have far too many apps on our phones, so it’s worth having a digital clear out every so often.

The more apps and services you give access to your personal information, the more potential ways there are for it to be exposed if an account or company is compromised.

Art Gilliland, of cyber firm Delinea, said: “Check which apps you’ve allowed to read your emails, see your contacts or access your files. Remove connections you no longer use. Don’t forget that deleting an app from your phone doesn’t necessarily cancel its access.”

It’s also worth reviewing the permissions of the apps you keep and switching off access to your camera, microphone, location or contacts if they don’t need it.

9. Regularly back-up files

Finally, don’t forget to back-up files on your phone or laptop. Doing this means you’ll still have access to important information if your device is damaged, lost or compromised in a cyber attack.

You can do this using a trusted cloud service or an external drive that isn’t permanently connected to your computer.

Mr Fothergill said: “Cyber attacks aren’t always about stealing money. Ransomware and malicious software can also lock you out of family photographs, important documents and personal records.”

Try to back-up your files regularly and check you can restore them if needed.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: EDF acquires UK rival in push to revive prepayment meters
data.description:
EDF has announced a deal to acquire Utilita, strengthening its position in the UK market by taking on the supplier’s 1.3 million customers.

The French state-owned energy firm announced the takeover of Utilita’s parent group, Luxion, on Thursday in a deal set to be completed next year.

EDF accounts for almost 10pc of the UK energy market and serves more than five million homes and businesses.

It is looking to expand further by acquiring Utilita, which was founded in 2003 and specialises in prepayment meters.

More than 90pc of Utilita’s customers use pay-as-you-go meters, which can no longer be forcibly installed after a government crackdown three years ago.

This stemmed from an exposé revealing that agents working for British Gas were breaking into vulnerable customers’ homes to install prepayment meters.

EDF is understood to be preparing for a greater up-tick in prepayment meters as energy bills surge.

Cornwall Insight predicted on Wednesday that the typical household’s annual gas and electricity costs could climb to £2,166 at the start of next year, a £443 increase from the current level.

The deal remains subject to regulatory approval and the two companies will remain independent until that is granted.

Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF in the UK, said: “This is a significant step in our ambition to grow EDF’s UK customer business.

“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us.”

Bill Bullen, the chief executive of Utilita, said the agreement “builds on an established relationship between the companies, following the successful transfer of 47,000 of Utilita’s residential customers to EDF in November 2025”.

The deal comes amid warnings that Britain’s household energy debt is projected to rise from £5.5bn to £7bn by the end of the year, with at least two million households struggling to keep up with their gas and electricity bills, according to trade body Energy UK.

Some suppliers and analysts have blamed the suspension of forced prepayment meter installations for the recent increase in energy debts.

Prepayment meters automatically disconnect energy supplies unless they are topped up.

Meanwhile, EDF’s proposed acquisition of Utilita comes amid broader consolidation across the UK energy sector.

Eon’s takeover of Ovo Energy was confirmed just last month, adding roughly four million customers to the German energy giant.

data.title: Police recover stolen orangutan statue
data.description:
A two-month police hunt for a large statue of an orangutan that was stolen from a Cambridgeshire garden centre by a “prolific thief” has ended in success.

CCTV caught the moment a man walked through the front doors of Scotsdales Garden Centre, in Horningsea, with the figure before cycling away with it propped up on his handlebars.

Cambridgeshire Constabulary said earlier this month that Derek Lundgren, 61, had been jailed for the Sept 7 theft, but that officers had not found the £799 statue.

In an update on Friday the force said that “thanks to a member of the public, the giant animal figure has been found”.

In a social media post, they wrote: “Following coverage of Lundgren’s conviction, information was received that an address in Teversham would be worth a look.

“Sure enough, the stolen orangutan was there and a woman was arrested. She has since been handed a conditional caution after admitting to receiving stolen goods.

“The ape, nicknamed Bruce by officers, will now be returned to the garden centre.”

Lundgren, of New Road, Sawston, pleaded guilty to theft from a shop and breaching three suspended sentences earlier this month. He was sentenced at Ipswich magistrates’ court to a year and 11 months in prison.

data.title: Energy bills expected to jump by £443 in January
data.description:
Annual household energy bills will jump by £443 in January to their highest level since 2023, according to a new forecast.

It means the average household’s annual gas and electricity costs would hit £2,166 at the start of next year, Cornwall Insight said on Wednesday. That is 26pc higher than the current level of £1,723, announced in October.

The energy consultancy blamed the painful midwinter hit on the Iran war keeping wholesale gas prices high.

Difficulties getting liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has left European storage tanks at record early-winter lows, prompting a scramble for higher-priced supplies.

Craig Lowrey, an analyst at Cornwall Insight, said: “Events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.”

Cornwall has raised its forecast from an earlier prediction of a 16pc increase in the January cap, which would have kept the average bill just below £2,000.

Although exporters have found ways to shift crude oil out of the Gulf, there is no alternative for LNG exports – and Iran is still attacking vessels as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

European gas prices have dropped to €83 (£69) per megawatt hour from more than €100 in late October but are still more than 160pc higher than before the war.

The hefty increase is a setback for John Healey, the Chancellor, after he vowed to get energy costs down last month.

Mr Lowrey said government initiatives, such as a £100 household energy payment and the removal of VAT from electricity charges “can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East”.

He urged the Government to look for ways to “control how exposed we are to these shocks in the future”, especially by decoupling energy costs from global gas prices.

Ofgem, the energy regulator, is poised to unveil its price cap next Wednesday.

The higher price cap is likely to be a double-blow for poorer households: it will also power even faster inflation, putting pressure on interest rates.

Inflation hit a one-year high of 3.6pc in October, driven by higher petrol prices and a 4pc increase in the energy price cap last month.

data.title: Deutsche handled almost $600m of suspicious payments linked to Epstein
data.description:
Germany’s largest bank handled nearly $600m (£455m) of suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, a figure far higher than previously thought.

Epstein was a long-standing client of Deutsche Bank, the country’s largest and best-known lender, after the bank took him on in 2013, despite his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor.

Internal documents show that Deutsche filed suspicious activity reports (SARs) in the US in 2019 identifying $582m of money transfers – more than double the amount previously known.

SARs are confidential alerts that banks must file with the authorities when they suspect a payment or customer could be linked to money laundering, fraud or other financial crime.

The SARs covered payments to women and suspected misuse of charitable donations, the Financial Times (FT) reported.

The value of the transfers is substantially higher than the sum disclosed in August after an investigation by the US Senate finance committee.

Investigators for US Senator Ron Wyden, who wrote the committee’s report, said at the time that Deutsche had flagged more than $250m in suspicious wire transfers flowing in and out of Epstein’s accounts.

The difference could reflect the wider scope of Deutsche’s investigation, which covered about 3,200 payments, the FT said.

The revelations emerged on Tuesday following the leak by whistleblowers of about 15 million internal files from Deutsche.

After he was forced out by JPMorgan Chase in 2013, Epstein followed his long-standing banker to Deutsche Bank.

The paedophile financier’s banker estimated that the relationship could eventually generate $2m to $4m a year from cash transfers of $100m to $300m or more, the FT said, but in reality it was worth far less.

The lender decided to terminate its relationship with Epstein only at the end of 2018, when renewed media coverage drew attention to his sexual abuse of girls and young women.

Epstein was found dead in his US jail cell in 2019.

Shares in Deutsche fell 6pc on Tuesday after the FT’s revelations from the whistleblower leak.

Deutsche has paid more than $200m in fines and settlements for its past dealings with Epstein without admitting wrongdoing.

The anonymous whistleblowers said in a statement that they were motivated by the “public interest”, adding that the bank needed a “complete overhaul in management and culture”.

A spokesman for Deutsche said: “As we said in 2020, the bank acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him.

“We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the US Congress regarding their investigations, and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

data.title: How Biden’s former aide sparked a $100bn stock market sell-off
data.description:
Walking down a street in New York filming a video, Sam Koppelman was about to detonate a $100bn (£76bn) bomb underneath Wall Street’s largest tech companies.

In a short video posted on X, the 30-year-old former speechwriter for Joe Biden said he had big news which was about to rock the AI sector.

He revealed that his hedge fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had published a new investigation into Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), a Silicon Valley tech giant.

The lengthy report alleged that AMD had continued to supply microchips to a Chinese server manufacturer, IEIT Systems, after the Asian group was blacklisted by US authorities.

AMD has denied any wrongdoing, claiming Hunterbrook’s report “misrepresents AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

However, its publication triggered a $100bn slump in the share price of the chip giant, contributing to a gloom engulfing the tech sector after the Nvidia scandal.

But who is Koppelman? And how did he and his hedge fund cause a tech crash?

The fund was launched two years ago and described itself as a “new kind of investigative newsroom”, which makes money by trading on stories it uncovers. Often by “shorting” companies to profit when their share prices fall.

Koppelman started the firm with Nathaniel Horowitz, his friend from Harvard University.

The two founders had graduated from the Ivy League institution only a few years ago and might well be considered scions of America’s liberal elite.

Koppelman, a native New Yorker, is the son of Brian Koppelman, the film and TV writer who wrote the 2007 film Ocean’s 13 starring George Clooney and Brad Pitt.

Hollywood star Matt Damon is said to have written a recommendation to Harvard in favour of Koppelman.

His school, the Ethical Culture Fieldston School, is also well known as one of New York’s best. He once even dated Maude Apatow, the American actress who is the daughter of Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann.

Horowitz, meanwhile, is the son of two Pulitzer Prize-winning writers. Tony Horwitz, his father, is best known for his investigations into the conditions of America’s low-paid workers, while Geraldine Brooks, his mother, won the prize for her novel March, about the US civil war.

He attended school in Martha’s Vineyard, the small island off the coast of Massachusetts where Barack Obama now owns an $11.75m holiday home, before studying Molecular and Cellular Biology.

He went on to start a series of biotech startups, focused on making treatments for diseases including pancreatic cancer and Type 1 diabetes, with the backing of some of the world’s biggest pharmaceutical firms.

Both Koppelman and Horowitz were politically minded from early on, with the pair having once co-written an article for the Harvard Crimson, criticising the elitism of some of Harvard’s exclusive, male-only “final clubs”.

In another article for the student newspaper, Horowitz described Donald Trump as “an existential threat to our country”.

Koppelman also worked as a speechwriter for both Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire founder of Bloomberg, and Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential campaign.

After graduating, the pair went on to start their own charity, Mayday Health, in response to the US Supreme Court’s decision to overturn the landmark Roe vs Wade ruling in 2022, which allowed US states to ban abortion.

The non-profit aims to use “guerrilla marketing” tactics to distribute information about accessing abortion pills. A strategy that draws some parallels to the ones used by Hunterbrook in its own campaigns.

The investigation into AMD has put Hunterbrook on the map in the often mysterious world of hedge funds and short-sellers, at a particularly gloomy time for the tech industry.

Recent years have even seen the closures of famous short sellers including Scion Asset Management, the hedge fund started by Michael Burry, who was depicted by Christian Bale in the 2015 film The Big Short.

Amid mounting concerns about the AI bubble, Hunterbrook could be just the first of a new wave of short sellers to profit from the tech slump.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Norway’s oil and gas supplies to plummet in threat to Britain’s energy
data.description:
Britain faces a massive blow to its energy supplies because of a slump in production in Norway.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday that Norway’s gas production will plummet by one third over the next decade and the Nordic country accounts for 40pc of total UK gas supplies.

Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst at Panmure Liberum, said the coming falls in Norwegian output will be “massively problematic” for the UK and drive up household bills.

Norway also accounts for 69pc of all gas imported into Britain, primarily through pipelines that run across the North Sea.

The IEA’s forecast follows a September report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, a government agency that monitors the nation’s reserves, which warned gas production may “fall steeply” from as early as 2030.

This is because new discoveries have not been large enough to maintain current production levels and the output of several major fields will soon decline.

Output at Troll, which is the largest gas field on the Norwegian continental shelf and feeds into the UK’s subsea pipelines, “will plateau rapidly post-2026”, it said.

Mr Kelty warned that the UK will be forced to import more liquefied natural gas (LNG), which is far more expensive.

He said: “The Government seems to think that it is all going to be fine because they’re going to build enough windmills.

“But the grid is not going to be updated quickly enough to compensate for that, so it is just going to mean that the UK has to buy more LNG from the US or Qatar, and that is certainly much more costly.”

LNG is more expensive than pipeline imports because the gas must be compressed and then re-gasified.

The UK and Europe will also be competing with Asian buyers, meaning the region will become even more exposed to global price shocks.

The European Union, which also imports large volumes of gas from Norway, is arguably even more exposed than the UK because it has relatively fewer LNG imports, Mr Kelty said.

The IEA said the decline in Norwegian gas production will be so large that overall gas production in Europe will slump by 13pc by 2035 despite the commissioning of new offshore developments in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean.

Norwegian oil production will also fall by around 30pc by 2035, while the UK’s oil output will sink by 45pc.

Mr Kelty said the numbers highlighted the need for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to give the greenlight for Rosebank in the North Sea.

Mr Kelty said: “It shows that it is absolute lunacy not to develop our own domestic resources. Energy security is key. We have access to oil and gas close to home.”

Mr Burnham signed off on drilling at the Jackdaw gasfield last month, but is yet to announce a decision on Rosebank.

Both fields were given the go-ahead for development under the Conservative government but were then blocked by legal challenges from climate campaign groups.

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Two-tier safety regulations are strangling Britain’s housebuilding
data.description:
The Canada Water redevelopment plan is perhaps the most ambitious construction project in London. The first new London town in 50 years, it promises thousands of homes, millions of square feet of retail and office space, new streets and a town square.

The capital and the economy desperately need this sort of shot in the arm. But the scheme is now in deep trouble.

Rising costs, high inflation and interest rates, and weakening demand have put the second phase of the plans on hold, throwing the £3.6bn development into chaos.

You’ll see plenty of headlines blaming the economic weather, but there’s a truth that nobody wants to confront. The Canada Water scheme didn’t die by accident: it was killed off by government regulation.

The worsening housing market that dealt the coup de grâce was only the last of a series of blows, many of them dealt by government policy.

British Land has been trying to break ground in Canada Water since 2005, only for the financial crisis to hit the pause button. It was restarted in 2014, but it took six years for Phase 1 to begin. Such things take time, but lengthy consultation processes and wrangling held up the project until it had been shaken down for a massive 35pc “affordable housing” target.

Finally ready to go in 2020, Covid lockdowns caused matters to be delayed once again. And just as things went back to normal, in 2023, the Government brought in stringent new fire safety requirements that required the entire development to be redesigned.

The result was to further delay and reduce the viability of the project, leading the affordable housing target to be lowered to 9pc in a desperate last-ditch attempt to save the project.

Some of the new measures were sensible, but the most costly – and least rational – was the requirement for two stairwells in every structure above 18m.

This requirement made Britain an international outlier. In Europe and Asia, mid-rise apartments commonly have a single stairwell, and in France, Germany, Singapore, China and Sweden, the requirements only come in for buildings of around 50-60m, which would have covered a building the height of Grenfell in any case.

Indeed, we know that three central problematic features of the Grenfell disaster were nothing to do with the stairwell. The flammable cladding, of course, which is now rightly banned, allowed a fire to spread that would not have otherwise. A modern sprinkler system would have put out the fire in the first place but was absent. The fire doors would have given residents time to evacuate, but these failed because of poor maintenance by the council.

Beyond some minor adjustments to the cladding, none of these issues would have applied to Canada Water’s apartments, which, like all new high-rises, would have been equipped with sprinklers and brand new fire doors. A failure born entirely of the negligence of the state, and the age of Grenfell, is now being offloaded on to private developments.

In the US, there is emerging research which suggests that restrictive second stairwell requirements there have made construction more expensive and reduced floorspace, without demonstrably improving safety.

In fact, the British Government has done nothing to require existing high-rises to implement the most effective fire safety system – a sprinkler system (estimated to be 99pc effective by the London Fire Brigade) – while making it harder and more expensive to build the modern apartment blocks that would have them by default.

We’ve made new housing too safe to build. By loading excessive safety requirements on to new builds, we are slowing the roll-out of modern fire safety systems and trapping millions of people in unsafe, ageing buildings. It’s estimated that more than a million people live in apartments at risk of fire and as many as eight million live in homes that are in some way dangerous.

When we make it too costly to build safer homes by adding redundant safety measures, it’s those lives that we’re putting at risk.
