data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Ofgem launches urgent inquiry into power grid delays
data.description:
Britain’s energy watchdog has launched an urgent inquiry into plans to accelerate electricity grid connections after they inadvertently caused more delays.

Ofgem said on Thursday it would investigate why an overhaul designed to speed up access to the grid had instead made it harder to secure a connection.

Developers have complained about lengthy waits to have their sites hooked up to electricity, which has stalled the rollout of new factories and homes.

The regulator said it shared the “frustration” of developers, acknowledging the outcomes from its reforms were “not good enough”.

The National Energy System Operator had been tasked with weeding out so-called “zombie projects” from a queue of schemes waiting for a connection.

However, Ofgem said that “the majority of projects in the reformed queue are seeing delays rather than advancements”.

Akshay Kaul, the energy watchdog’s director-general for infrastructure, said that the connection dates offered to too many projects were “not good enough”.

“Our inquiry will establish transparently what has driven these delays,” he said.

The inquiry came as Labour moved to scrub all mention of its controversial 2030 green energy policy from an announcement hailing the latest round of net zero subsidies.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero on Thursday appeared to distance itself further from a target to run the UK’s electricity grid entirely on low-carbon technologies by the end of the decade.

Known as Clean Power 2030, the proposal was a centrepiece of Labour’s election manifesto and championed by Ed Miliband, who became energy secretary.

However, the policy appears to have been dropped from government communications after an announcement on new wind and solar farm subsidies omitted the reference.

It comes after Mr Miliband was moved to the Foreign Office this summer, replaced by Miatta Fahnbulleh as Energy Secretary.

His departure was quickly followed by that of Chris Stark, appointed by Mr Miliband to oversee the Clean Power 2030 programme.

Ministers still refer to “clean power”, but they set no date and are pledging to reform the system to focus on costs rather than timelines.

It follows warnings from John Healey, the Chancellor, that while he supported clean power “we will only buy projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security”.

Michael Shanks, the energy minister, has also said future clean power projects had to prioritise lower bills.

“These reforms … make the auction process more transparent and competitive, so we secure the best projects at the best price for consumers,” he said.

The shift in emphasis from decarbonisation by 2030 to cutting prices is likely to mean fewer applications or approvals for new renewables projects.

These have always been heavily reliant on subsidies in the form of Contracts for Difference.

However, the latest auction round set no effective budget for the subsidies, leaving developers uncertain of the funding.

data.title: Financier caught up in row with neighbours over basement golf simulator
data.description:
A financier has won planning permission to dig 4m under his driveway to build a golf simulator and games room, despite objections from neighbours.

Tim Woolford secured permission to install a basement below the drive of his modern home. The underground room will be 13ft 1in deep and have a simulator, bar area and pool table.

Neighbours in Winchester, Hampshire, where homes are worth an average of £1m, say they have environmental concerns about the project and that the works will affect their lives for months.

Residents have referred to Mr Woolford’s home as the “Lego house”, because of its striking modern design, and say it is not in keeping with traditional properties in the area.

Winchester City Council has approved the plans with conditions, despite a planning officer recommending it be refused.

Mr Woolford, his wife and their two children have lived in the house since the coronavirus pandemic and, in drawing up an underground extension, had sought to create an extension plan that would have the least impact on neighbours.

He said: “Our view was that we wanted to do something that would impact people the absolute least as possible. Some of the people that objected misunderstood what would be here when the builders were done.”

Mr Woolford, who is managing director of a finance-management company in London, said he and his wife would still be able to park on the driveway when the building work was completed, so this would not affect the on-street parking.

He said he wanted to build the space for his two sons, who are aged seven and eight, and wanted to install a golf simulator, because they were interested in the sport.

Mr Woolford said: “We have kids that are growing, and it is good for them. We didn’t actually think there would be any discussions about the plans. We did quite a few developments to the house a few years ago, and arguably this has been more contentious.”

He said one of his sons played the guitar and he thought it would be less disruptive to allow him to play in the basement extension – sometimes referred to as an iceberg basement.

Mr Woolford said: “People go into their lofts and convert garages, and I didn’t want to go into the loft and put big windows, and I don’t have a garage to convert.”

He said the process should be reasonably quick and should not cause very much disruption to the neighbours.

He said: “It is actually a quick build. The soil can be taken out within a week. We should be done in about 10 to 12 weeks, so much more minimal than people expect.”

Mr Woolford said the complaints were a “group effort” and they came from houses further down the street, who were not as affected by the works. As well as being 4m deep, the new basement will be 9.5m in width, and 10.9m in length.

Hazel Agombar, who has lived in the street for 20 years, said the house was already referred to as the “Lego house” and she did not think more work should be done to it.

She said: “I didn’t want it to set a precedent of people applying for basement extensions because of the disruption. We have people who are wheelchair users regularly using this street. There is limited parking up the top.

“This is a lovely street, people get on. It’s very green and leafy, and I just thought it was a poor reason to try to change the character of it and try to navigate that disruption.”

Mrs Agombar said that she thought the decision contravened the council’s local plan to make Winchester more environmentally friendly. She said: “It seems to go against the new local plan. It is only one development but it seems like it is starting a precedent. It is for a golf simulation room.

“This is crazy. They have this massive house with a cinema room and garden. If you want a bigger house, maybe you should move if you want to dig up a conservation area.

“The council has allowed a highly intensive carbon footprint development. Digging up that drive is going to be hugely carbon intensive.”

Another objector is Keith Hatter, 79, who is blind and has lived on the street for the last 14 years.

He said: “The main reason was that it involves digging out to about 2.5m of the ground in front of the house, and I am slightly worried that this might have an effect on the soil structure.”

Mr Hatter added: “The second objection I have come to second-hand – because I am totally blind – is that it might interfere with the character. It would involve the trees and general flora in front of the house being removed and have a slightly detrimental environmental effect.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.

data.title: AI solves 167-year-old maths problem, Anthropic researcher claims
data.description:
A researcher at Anthropic has claimed that AI has solved a 167-year-old mathematics puzzle.

Levent Alpöge, a mathematics expert and an employee at the US technology giant, said on Friday he had solved the Riemann hypothesis using Anthropic’s Claude chatbot.

The puzzle, widely regarded as one of the best-known problems in maths, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and whether they follow a precise hidden pattern.

It has gone unsolved since it was proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859.

Proving the hypothesis would represent a major academic breakthrough for the technology.

The puzzle is one of seven so-called Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m (£763,000) reward for anyone who solves it.

Commenting on his solution to the problem, Mr Alpöge said: “An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary.

“In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead.”

‘Greatest shock in my lifetime’

Generations of mathematicians have been confounded by the Riemann hypothesis, with Mr Alpöge’s claims sending shockwaves around the academic world.

Yang-Hui He, of the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences, said: “I thought it was inconceivable that it would be proven in my lifetime. All mathematicians see this as the Holy Grail of mathematics.”

Prof Jon Keating, a mathematical physicist at Oxford University, said: “This is the greatest shock in my lifetime.

“There have been AI breakthroughs in mathematics this year the likes of which I never thought I would see, but this is an enormous leap beyond even those.”

Mr Alpöge, a Turkish-American maths expert, said he had told Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, on Sunday night that he believed he had solved the puzzle.

This was just days before the company launched its record-breaking $2tn stock market listing in New York.

He said the problem had been the “sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood”.

The solution to the puzzle includes more than 17 million lines of mathematical code and is set to be pored over by mathematicians and rival AI labs to confirm the proof.

AI giants have laid claim to a series of academic breakthroughs in maths, biology and physics this year as increasingly advanced systems tackle unsolved problems.

A row broke out between researchers at OpenAI and Prof Tristan Buckmaster in September after the AI lab announced the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a 90-year-old maths puzzle.

Prof Buckmaster claimed OpenAI had tried to pressure him into working together on a solution when he was close to his own breakthrough.

The breakthrough with the Riemann hypothesis is set to prompt fresh soul-searching among academics as AI tools tackle problems that some experts have dedicated their lives to solving.

It will also renew focus on the speed of AI developments as labs spend substantial sums on pointing their bots towards scientific or mathematical mysteries.

Anthropic has previously warned that its AI is approaching the point where it can improve itself autonomously.

data.title: FTSE energy giant quits North Sea over tax raids
data.description:
A British energy giant has quit the North Sea after Labour’s windfall taxes and drilling bans made its operations unviable.

EnQuest, which is listed on the London stock market, said on Wednesday that it had sold its entire UK operation to Neo Next+, a relative newcomer to the North Sea, for a knock-down price of $960m (£730m).

It plans to move its investments to south-east Asia after quitting British waters.

The FTSE 250 company’s UK operations include the giant Magnus and Kraken fields, 1,000 km of key subsea pipelines and the Sullom Voe terminal in Shetland.

EnQuest’s decision follows an industry backlash against John Healey’s decision to keep a windfall tax on North Sea oil and gas profits in place until 2030 despite pressure to scrap it.

Labour’s initial extension of the windfall tax from 2028 to 2030 under Ed Miliband left EnQuest facing a $124m bill, it revealed on Wednesday, pushing the company into a $2m loss for the year.

This was in addition to an $84m bill it paid in 2025, which was much higher than expected after Labour abolished some tax allowances. The windfall tax added another $24m to its tax bill in the first half of this year, alongside $28m in other levies.

Amjad Bseisu, EnQuest’s chief executive, blamed an “uncertain investment environment within the UK”.

The company said it would instead focus on its operations in south-east Asia, aiming to recycle “invested capital from a high-tax, low-return basin into a high-growth region that is structurally short on energy”.

EnQuest’s decision means Neo Next+ will consolidate its position as the North Sea’s largest oil and gas producer.

John Knight, the founder and executive chair of the private equity firm, said: “The addition of EnQuest’s UK oil and gas business further strengthens our scale and resilience in the UK North Sea, while adding production, reserves and cash flow to our portfolio.”

EnQuest is among the UK’s top producers of oil and gas, producing the equivalent of 31,000 barrels of oil a day last year with reserves approaching another 500 million barrels.

Its untapped Bressay and Bentley fields are among the largest in UK waters, capable of producing up to 600 million barrels of oil.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “The devastating news that EnQuest is withdrawing from the UK is the latest sign that this Government’s policies on oil and gas are hanging a ‘closed for business’ sign over the North Sea.

“We are in the midst of an energy crisis but Labour is still banning licences and maintaining windfall taxes. We need to open the North Sea, abolish the windfall tax and get Britain drilling.”

EnQuest is is the latest energy firm to leave UK waters over Labour’s windfall tax. BP has also announced plans to sell all its UK offshore assets, with the final date for bids due in early December.

Meg O’Neill, BP’s boss, linked the decision to the UK tax regime.

data.title: Swiss face £9bn bill to keep trains running on time
data.description:
Switzerland’s trains are celebrated for their immaculate punctuality. But now the country is facing a £9bn bill to stop its rail services becoming like those in Germany, its erratic neighbour.

The country’s largest railway operator, state-owned SBB, has said its backlog of repairs to tracks and signal boxes rose 12pc last year to 9.5bn Swiss francs (£8.6bn).

If the repairs aren’t carried out, SBB has warned that Switzerland risks “a situation similar to that in other countries” – a reference to Germany, where the formerly clockwork-like train network has become notoriously unreliable.

So far, the Swiss trains are holding the line on their fabled punctuality. This year 94pc of its trains have arrived within three minutes of their scheduled time, about the same rate as the previous two years.

No other major European country gets above 90pc, and many have resorted to using a looser definition of punctuality.

Britain scored 84pc last year. Germany clocked 88pc, but that excludes cancelled trains and defines punctual as within six minutes. Even on that metric, just 60pc of Germany’s long-distance and high-speed trains run on time.

Germany’s decline arose from underinvestment in maintenance. As it tries to play catch-up, large sections of track often have to be closed for repairs, making punctuality even worse.

Switzerland will be keen to avoid that fate.

But SBB is at loggerheads with the Swiss government, which instead wants to spend 20bn Swiss francs (CHF).on expanding and embellishing the rail network.

This could include building a whole new station at Lucerne, at a potential cost of more than CHF 3bn, and a 17-mile tunnel with a potential budget of CHF 800m.

SBB, in a submission to a public consultation, urged the authorities to prioritise fixing the existing network over any major expansion.

Both sides agree, though, that the signalling system also needs a technological overhaul that will cost a further CHF 9bn.

This week SBB kicked off the first CHF 2bn tender for the IT revamp. The full digitalisation of signalling will cost another CHF 7bn by 2045, but so far the government has budgeted just CHF 1bn for this process.

Meanwhile, money is tight for the essential repairs to keep the trains running on time. SBB has said it needs to repair at least 143 miles of track a year, but last year only managed 116 miles.

Funding for its track and signalling work comes from a separate Rail Infrastructure Fund, which is bankrolled by annual contributions from the national and cantonal governments, alongside some hypothecated portions of VAT, income tax and the mineral oil tax. Some of this funding is due to expire in 2030.

data.title: BBC scraps Room on the Broom over Walliams abuse allegations
data.description:
The BBC has removed an adaptation of Dame Julia Donaldson’s children’s book Room On The Broom featuring David Walliams.

The broadcaster withdrew the animated 2012 film from platforms such as iPlayer as part of a review of “all material” featuring and written by the comedian following the publication of sex abuse allegations.

Walliams, 55, a children’s author and former Britain’s Got Talent (BGT) judge, was named as part of an alleged sexual misconduct investigation by The Guardian and ITV News on Tuesday.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”, while several women accused him of “grooming” them when they were teenagers. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

On Friday, the Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of non-recent “serious” sex offence allegations against him “in recent days”.

Earlier in the week, the BBC said it was carrying out a content review on its platforms and was in the process of “removing” some.

In Room On The Broom, Walliams voices a frog, alongside Gillian Anderson as a witch and Simon Pegg as the narrator.

His character has just three lines in the 30-minute film, along with some “ribbits”.

In one line, his character says: “I am a frog, as clean as can be. Is there room on the broom for a frog like me?”

A BBC spokesman said: “These are serious allegations. As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is under way.”

Walliams rose to fame working alongside Matt Lucas on the BBC sketch comedy series Little Britain, which ran from 2003 until 2006.

They then created and starred in Come Fly With Me, which aired on the BBC for one season in 2010.

Both shows are currently unavailable on iPlayer, as is a 2020 episode of Who Do You Think You Are? featuring Walliams.

Adaptations of his best-selling children’s books, including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, are also unavailable on the service.

Channel 4 and Sky also axe Walliams content

Other broadcasters have also removed programming featuring Walliams from their streaming services.

Channel 4 has taken down episodes of 8 Out Of 10 Cats Does Countdown and the 2021 special Chitty Flies Again with Walliams.

Sky also removed Walliams’s work from its platform and dropped the distribution of the upcoming film Fing! based on his 2019 children’s book.

In a statement, a Sky spokesman said: “The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK and Ireland licensee of Fing!

“We have already removed content which features him from our platforms.”

Angel Studios confirmed it would still release the film in the US, but a cameo featuring Walliams would be removed and he would not take part in its promotion.

Walliams has not yet responded to Tuesday’s reports in The Guardian or ITV News.

But in a letter understood to have been sent several months ago to journalists working on the investigations, he denied being a “sexual predator”.

Walliams said he recognised he “behaved thoughtlessly” at times, and regretted not taking people’s feelings “properly into account”, but insisted he had not broken the law.

The ITV and The Guardian reports about Walliams followed his unsuccessful attempts to seek an injunction to prevent the media revealing his identity – with his lawyers arguing there was a risk he would take his own life after two previous suicide attempts.

Several sources alleged inappropriate behaviour towards women at the prime-time show BGT, where Walliams served as a judge from 2012 to 2022, and at his publisher HarperCollins, which dropped him last year.

The allegations also led to Walliams being dropped by his literary agency, Independent Talent Group.

Representatives for Dame Julia were contacted for comment.

data.title: Britain can’t afford any more quangos
data.description:
Who says Andy Burnham doesn’t do anything of significance? In the last few days, his Government has created “water councils” to supervise an industry that is already collapsing under the weight of over-regulation, as well as a “special health authority” to absorb staff from NHS England.

At this rate, we are well on track for a hundred or more new regulatory, supervisory or advisory bodies a year, each one equipped with generously paid staff and swish London offices, plus the obligatory satellite branch in Bolton. 

This is crazy. The British economy can’t afford all the quangos – we should be abolishing them instead.

If you happen to have some spare time on your hands, and feel like a cushy gig, I recommend applying for one of the new water councils.

Apparently there will be eight of them across the country, designed, in the words of Burnham, to give local people “a real say over what they need from their water company”.

Never mind that we already have one water regulator, Ofwat, with an annual budget of £78m, as well as consultative bodies, such as Water Resources East, not to mention the whole series of financial regulators that all the regional water companies have to deal with.

It seems what we need is just one more layer of oversight.

Likewise, most of us might imagine that the answer to the question of “what do we need from our water company” would be pretty straightforward. Clean water, and enough of it that we can use the sprinklers in the garden over a hot summer, with fewer leaks, and lower bills. But, hey, whatever. It seems we don’t need more engineers, or reservoirs, or any of that stuff. We need a “council” where things can be “discussed”.

Similarly, some of us might have imagined that getting rid of NHS England would mean streamlining the health service. But no.

The Special Health Authority is designed to provide jobs for all the people who might otherwise lose them. It will probably be “special” for them, if not for patients.

Meanwhile, back in September, the Government announced the creation of the OneGov Delivery Agency, due for launch next spring, with a budget still to be determined, while Great British Railways has now been formally launched, with Sir John Kingman bringing all his commercial nous as a former permanent secretary to the Treasury to make trains “great” again.

It probably won’t be long before we see the launch of Great British Steel for all the nationalised metal-bashing assets.

The list goes on and on. It seems like a long time since Sir Keir Starmer – if anyone still remembers him – promised a “bonfire of the quangos”. Instead, the Government is launching new ones at an accelerating rate. There doesn’t seem to be any issue that ministers don’t think can be solved by a task force, a council or a special advisory committee.

The trouble is, none of them is actually going to make anything any better.

There are three big problems. To start with, the costs keep adding up. According to figures from the TaxPayer’s Alliance, 438 quangos received total funding of £378bn in the last full financial year.

Between them, they employ almost half a million people. True, some of that is money that the Government would have been spending anyway, except that it has been outsourced to a separate agency.

But each layer adds costs of its own. There are offices to be paid for, and consultants to be hired, and staff, complete with generous pensions, to be added to the payroll. Each one is, without question, more expensive than if the Government were simply doing the work directly.

Next, it means proliferating red tape. As soon as a new council or agency is created it has to keep itself busy. That only means one thing. It has to keep creating new regulations, and targets, followed by reports on their implementation, and fines for anyone who does not follow the rules.

Finally, all quangos expand. They have to build their empires, just like any organisation, and the only way they can do that is by taking on more people, and interfering even more with whatever industry they are meant to be looking after. We can see that very clearly in their budgets.

Why is Ofwat spending 9pc more this year than last year? It is hard to argue the water industry is 9pc better run.

Or why does the Office of Rail and Road need a 5.75pc budget increase, especially given that most of the rail industry has been taken back into state ownership, so it is hard to figure out why we even need it at all.

No quango in human history ever volunteered to close itself down, or for its funding to be reduced, and there is no chance that any Labour minister will ever demand that it does. Instead, they just expand relentlessly.

The British economy is turning into one giant regulatory body with a country attached.

It is crushing growth, stifling genuine entrepreneurship, and running up huge bills that the economy can barely afford. Even by the standards of this Labour Government, two new quangos in a single week is an alarming rate of increase. At best, they will absorb time and money, while making no positive difference to anything.

At worst, they will make each industry they meddle in even more hopelessly inefficient. The only solution is to sweep them all away – but unfortunately there is very little chance of that happening under this Government.

data.title: Anthropic lacks ‘basic moral compass’, say publishers
data.description:
Anthropic’s cavalier approach to copyright shows the AI giant “lacks a basic moral compass”, news publishers have said.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company after admissions in its stock market filing.

Anthropic, which went public on Thursday at a valuation of $1.5tn (£1.1tn), told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls and a system known as robots.txt, which tells web crawlers what pages they can access, but that this “may not always be successful”.

Anthropic also acknowledged that it might not be able to verify whether the material it used to train its models was protected by copyright.

Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said: “Anthropic’s IPO (initial public offering) filing confirms a chilling reality about how this new darling of the stock market operates.

“Paying for content should be a basic cost of doing business and investors should ask how long their new cash cow thinks it can go without paying its bills.

“If Anthropic’s lack of a basic moral compass does not give them pause for thought, the massive legal exposure should.”

Silicon Valley’s ‘hollow’ promises

Baroness Kidron, the crossbench peer and filmmaker who directed Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason, said the filing showed AI companies’ promises to respect copyright were “hollow”.

She said: “The only thing that has compelled it to make this confession is the pursuit of money through its IPO. But our laws should not be a victim of their greed.”

Copyright has emerged as a major flashpoint in AI amid accusations tech companies have used vast troves of data to train their models without permission.

Dame Caroline Dinenage, the chairman of the Commons culture, media and sport committee, accused Silicon Valley firms last year of the “largest copyright heist” in history.

At the same time, the rise of chatbots and Google’s AI summaries is diverting readers away from news sites, leading to sharp drops in online traffic.

The Telegraph is among a number of British news outlets that have joined forces to stop AI giants from cashing in on their journalism.

Anthropic and rivals including ChatGPT maker OpenAI have relied on “fair use” principles under copyright law to date.

But in filings published before its stock market debut this week, Anthropic acknowledged that the legality of this approach had not been “authoritatively resolved” by courts in the US and around the world.

AI companies are facing a wave of lawsuits from publishers and rights holders about alleged copyright infringement, with The New York Times suing both OpenAI and Perplexity.

Anthropic itself was forced last year to pay $1.5bn to settle a copyright claim about its use of pirated books, with Harry Potter publisher Bloomsbury among those to receive a payout.

The filing revealed that the company faces two further lawsuits from publishers in Canada which allege their journalism was used to train Claude models.

Other outlets, including Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp and The New York Times, have opted to sign licensing deals with AI developers for the use of their content.

Anthropic acknowledged that if it could not rely on the fair use defence, it might be required to pay “significant fees” to obtain a licence.

In the UK, Labour is facing a backlash against its plans to water down copyright laws to allow AI companies to scrape data unless rights holders explicitly opt out.

Baroness Kidron added: “Anthropic is built in part on other people’s property.

“Ministers should read this filing and ask themselves who they were protecting when they refused to give creators basic transparency and whether there is any justification to refuse it now they see the abuse of our law in black and white.”

Anthropic has been contacted for comment.

data.title: What opening a joint bank account taught me about my relationship
data.description:
How do you and your partner deal with joint expenses? Let us know in the comments or email money@telegraph.co.uk*.

If you had told me a year ago that £1 doughnuts would test my relationship with my partner, I wouldn’t have believed it.

My boyfriend Alex and I have been together for two-and-a-half years, yet because work keeps us in separate cities, we have never lived together. Recently, however, we decided to take a different kind of “next step” in our relationship: opening a joint bank account.

There were practical reasons for this, but I was also curious to see how our relationship, as yet untested by more traditional milestones such as marriage, would handle an experiment such as this.

We both thought we knew each other’s attitudes to money, but creating even a relatively small shared pot compels you to turn abstract ideas about fairness, ownership and compromise into actual rules.

We agreed to put the same amount of money into the account as and when it needs topping up. Household items and food we buy when staying together are considered joint expenses, along with train tickets or petrol for travelling to see each other.

Our foray into shared finances was going swimmingly until one day, I got a notification from the bank saying that £1 had just been spent on our joint card. My partner walked in the door a few minutes later, excited because he had just found a pack of five doughnuts on sale for – you guessed it – £1.

This was something that had come up in our relationship before: Alex, a committed saver, is often content to buy or eat whatever is cheapest, while I am more of a food (and everything else) snob who would sooner spend a few extra pounds.

I wasn’t annoyed at the money, but it did puzzle me that he considered this a joint purchase when he was the only one going to be eating them. Fearful of being petty, I decided to let the issue lie.

Yet soon enough, the same question started appearing everywhere. If Alex wants the cheapest toilet paper while I would sooner spring for something softer, should he have to subsidise my preference? If we buy chocolate from the joint account but he eats most of it, is that really a shared expense?

We might have known what we were getting into. Research published by Starling Bank last year found that 76pc of surveyed couples argued about money regardless of how they managed their finances.

Becky Palmano, a 38-year-old production executive based in Jersey, faced similar issues when she first combined finances with her now-husband, Sam, also 38.

Initially, she tells me, they thought they were alike in how they approached money.

Once they began making financial decisions together, this turned out not to be the case: “My attitude is quite ‘live now’, which can occasionally become ‘spend now’, whereas Sam is more inclined to plan ahead, save and deliberate over bigger decisions like trips.”

The couple have devised a strategy for dealing with financial “missteps”, which they call “idiot tax”. The couple keep a shared savings pot of around £5,000 to cover the financial consequences of either of them doing something stupid.

“Recently, I booked Sam on to entirely the wrong flight. Idiot tax,” says Palmano. “The basic rule is that if it’s a genuine mistake, you’re allowed to be annoyed, but you don’t get to turn it into a huge argument about the money. Whoever has messed up has to hold their hands up, admit they’ve been an idiot and, ideally, not do it again.”

She also spoke of an incident early on in their relationship where a disastrous weekend away resulted in a series of costly financial blunders, including a last-minute hire car (which then got damaged) and a speeding fine.

Ultimately, they decided to split the damage 50-50 after realising that sometimes, trying to establish exactly whose expense something is “becomes more ridiculous than the expense itself”.

This was a trap I had already fallen into with my partner. After an absurd discussion where we tried to calculate who was subsidising more of the other’s spending, we resolved to continue splitting things equally and save ourselves the trouble of accounting for every difference in consumption and salary.

Admittedly, this isn’t something I usually agree with. I have always felt that it is best to split things equitably, so if your partner earns more than you, then what they pay in terms of rent and household expenses should reflect that gap.

Yet the difference between our salaries is small – I would estimate that Alex earns £5,000 more than me annually, although it’s difficult to know for certain as we both take on ad-hoc work.

We agreed that for the time being, our relationship would be best served by letting the little things go.

Tom Desborough, a financial planner at Paradigm Norton, suggests that those with different attitudes to spending are not inherently incompatible. He finds most couples are willing to compromise a bit because it’s part of being in a loving relationship.

If you want to avoid being blindsided by your partner’s spending habits, however, he recommends asking more holistic questions early on in the relationship. For example, where do you see your life in 10 or 20 years’ time, or if you won the lottery, what would you do?

You may already know that you are both savers, but what you are saving your money for is just as important.

Desborough also recommends a “yours, mine and ours” approach, rather than pooling everything. It is a system Eduardo Gomes, 38, and his wife Carla, 44, eventually arrived at, although it took an expensive accidental purchase to get them there.

When they moved from Brazil to London, they combined their finances to cover rent and household costs, using a single credit card.

During Covid, Eduardo found an auction website and placed bids on five coffee machines, unexpectedly winning all five at a cost of around £1,000. Understandably, his wife wasn’t pleased. He managed to sell four of the machines for a profit, but they have since switched to having both joint and separate accounts.

Now, Gomes says, they have learned from each other’s attitudes; Carla has taught him the importance of having a savings buffer, especially as she now works part-time to spend more time with their young daughter, and he has encouraged her to be more adventurous.

“Ultimately, we complement each other’s spending behaviours,” he says.

This was another lesson Alex and I learned. We could have gone back and forth for hours over whose attitude to money was better, but ultimately, if we wanted to move forward, we needed to accept that there wasn’t going to be an outcome where either of us “wins”.

In that sense, combining even a small part of our finances became a useful trial run for the long-term relationship we hope to have. We might have spent ages debating fairness and compromise in the abstract, but we needed to put those ideas into practice to see how we would build a financial life together.

Of course, compromising over £1 doughnuts is one thing. Making bigger decisions down the line will be considerably harder. The important thing is that we understand each other’s respective money attitudes before we try.

data.title: Grid operator handed £1bn Treasury loan to meet soaring wasted wind costs
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has been forced to seek a £1bn loan from the Treasury to meet soaring wasted wind payments.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the body responsible for keeping the lights on, has been granted extra taxpayer support after the bill for so-called balancing costs hit £2bn this year.

That is up from £1.5bn in 2025. Neso has to commit ever-growing amounts to pay wind farms to switch off when the grid cannot cope with their output.

This is alongside payments to gas-fired power stations to replace lost power.

Neso confirmed its request for extra cash on Thursday, saying it had struck a “time-limited extension of a working capital facility from £700m to £1.7bn”.

It comes after the windy autumn weather pushed up balancing costs to £740m in October alone.

Typically, Neso recoups this money from energy bills. But balancing costs are now rising more quickly than the grid operator can recover the cash.

Wind farms are typically shut off because of transmission bottlenecks on the wires connecting Scottish turbines with households south of the border.

The low capacity of those transmission lines means excessive power can cause overheating, forcing turbines to be deactivated to avoid damage when it is too windy. Wind farm operators are then compensated as a result.

However, the main costs are incurred in paying gas-fired stations in southern England to fire up to compensate for the missing wind power.

This is always expensive but is currently made worse by the surge in gas prices caused by the Iran war.

The normal wholesale price of power is around £170 per megawatt hour, but Neso has been forced to pay significantly more over the past three months.

The Telegraph revealed earlier this month that Neso was paying around £1,500 per megawatt hour to at least three power stations.

‘Labour’s obsession with net zero’

Kathryn Porter, an analyst, said the costs had also been amplified by Neso’s failures to forecast supply and demand accurately.

She said: “The scale of the forecasting failure is extraordinary. Neso knows about transmission constraints and has forecasts of wind output and demand well before delivery.

“Where substantial wind curtailment is inevitable, arranging it in advance would allow wholesale prices to reflect the electricity that can actually be delivered.”

Balancing costs are common, but they have spiralled in the UK because so many wind farms were built in rural areas where there is not enough grid capacity to carry their output.

Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said: “This is yet another symptom of the failure to reform the electricity market, and it all falls on energy users at a time we’re already paying eye-watering prices.”

Richard Tice, Reform UK’s energy spokesman, said Labour’s focus on renewables such as wind power was exposing households and businesses to ever-greater costs.

He said: “Grid operator Neso has to borrow £1bn more from Treasury to keep the lights on by paying double: compensating wind farms not to turn off and begging gas generators to turn on.

“This is entirely due to Labour’s obsession with net zero that is making everyone poorer and killing jobs.”

Neso said the Treasury loan did not reflect the organisation’s underlying financial position.

A spokesman said: “We have agreed an extension to our working capital arrangements, allowing current balancing tariffs to remain unchanged and providing predictability for suppliers and their customers for the remainder of the charging year.”

John Constable, of the Renewable Energy Foundation, said: “Neso is having to borrow to pay a constraint bill that has spiralled because successive governments connected wind farms far faster than the grid needed to carry their output.

“The only lasting reform is to stop compensating wind generators for constraints they could have foreseen, so that the cost falls on developers rather than on bill payers and now taxpayers.”

data.title: London house prices suffer worst drop since financial crisis
data.description:
Property prices in inner London have suffered the worst drop since the financial crisis as higher mortgage rates slow the capital’s housing market.

A toxic cocktail of soaring borrowing costs, high levels of stamp duty and the looming mansion tax caused central London property prices to slump 7.2pc in the 12 months to September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It means the average price of a home in inner London’s 12 boroughs and the City – which includes areas such as Camden, Tower Hamlets, Newham and Lambeth – dropped by just over £48,000 in a year, falling from £669,532 to £621,491.

However, the data revealed there was a significant divide in the areas of the capital where property prices fell. Outer London boroughs recorded just a 0.1pc decline in the price of a home in the 12 months to September.

On average, property prices across the capital dropped 3.5pc in the year to September.

Jonathan Hopper, the chief executive of Garrington Property Finders, said: “This huge divergence reflects the gulf between the buyers typically drawn to the two areas. Demand in outer London comes largely from domestic buyers, and while this has softened over the past year, it has been resilient.”

He warned that in stark contrast “a series of punitive tax increases”, including the looming mansion tax, had dented demand in inner London, with wealthy, international buyers reconsidering whether to purchase property.

Despite the slump, official figures showed that average UK house prices increased by 1.2pc, to £273,000.

London and the South East were the only two regions in the UK to record a drop in annual house prices, the data from the ONS showed.

The capital will be the hardest hit by Labour’s upcoming mansion tax, also known as the high-value property surcharge. The levy will hit properties worth £2m or more with a surcharge of at least £2,500 a year when it comes into effect in April 2028.

Wealthy areas of inner London have also recorded double-digit declines in annual property prices as they grapple with the effect of the scrapping of non-dom status and higher stamp duty rates.

House prices in Kensington and Chelsea declined 15.6pc year on year to an average of £1.17m in September 2026, down from £1.39m, according to Land Registry data.

In Westminster, house prices dropped 18.5pc in the year to September, with the average property costing £861,130, compared to £1.06m in September 2025.

Inner London’s flat market has also experience a significant slowdown, as average flat prices dropped 8.5pc. This compared with a 2.6pc decline in the price of detached properties over the same period.

Despite the fall in property prices in the capital, prospective buyers will still feel the squeeze, as borrowing costs have risen sharply since the outbreak of the Iran war, adding hundreds to mortgage repayments.

Paige Tao, an economist at PwC UK, said: “First time buyers entering the market with smaller deposits are more exposed to higher mortgage rates, while those who have moved out of their childhood home face the added challenge of saving for a deposit.”

data.title: ‘Saks f---ed with my mum’: The millionaire on a mission to take down store giant
data.description:
A millionaire is paying protesters to picket a luxury New York department store that he claims fired his mother after a customer attacked her.

Jeffrey Vinokur, 36, said the daily protests outside Saks Fifth Avenue would go on “for as long as it takes” until justice was served.

He is demanding that the company’s chief executive apologise publicly and an outside investigation be launched and has also called on New York to change its employment laws to protect workers who are victims of crime.

The protests started last Thursday – just before Saks’s busiest season – with women holding signs saying: “BEATEN AT SAKS. THEN FIRED. I WANT ANSWERS.”

Mr Vinokur, an entrepreneur who sold his education-tech company for $100m (£79m) last year, doubled the number of picketers this week from 15 to 30 to increase pressure on the company.

“I can go on for years – that’s what scares Saks the most,” Mr Vinokur told The Telegraph. “They’re not going to get away with it.”

Saks, once an icon of American luxury, has in recent years been plagued by falling sales and financial woes that led to Saks Global’s bankruptcy filing in January and subsequent restructuring. Its prestige, in turn, has suffered.

Laza Susuni, Mr Vinokur’s 62-year-old mother, had been a new sales associate at its 10-floor flagship store in Midtown Manhattan when she reported being attacked on June 28.

The incident began with a customer asking Ms Susuni where to find a fashion brand. When Ms Susuni asked the price point, she claimed the customer became enraged and demanded she be instantly fired.

A verbal dispute followed. The customer allegedly then began harassing and recording Ms Susuni in a dressing room area, where her manager had instructed her to wait while she spoke with the customer.

The situation escalated when Ms Susuni also took her phone out to record.

According to Ms Susuni’s police report, the customer then punched her in the face with a closed fist and kicked her in the stomach.

A photograph showed her being taken to hospital in an ambulance with minor injuries.

The customer was arrested and charged with five counts of assault and harassment, according to police and court documents. She pleaded guilty to a misdemeanour and was released.

Five days after the incident, Ms Susuni was fired by Saks.

“I was betrayed by the company. It was just horrific,” she told The Telegraph. “My safety, dignity and wellbeing was violated… But there was no justice for me being attacked.”

In her termination letter, seen by The Telegraph, Saks wrote that the decision was a “result of serious policy violations and insubordinate behaviour”, citing her using her phone to record.

“Your lack of judgment and inappropriate conduct directly escalated a situation with a customer and resulted in a physical altercation, and endangered the safety of yourself and others,” the letter read.

Mr Vinokur accused Saks – which is managed by Exemplar Luxury Group, a holding company which also owns luxury department stores Bergdorf Goodman and Neiman Marcus – of treating his mother as a “disposable minimum-wage worker”.

He cast it as a David versus Goliath battle. “It’s kind of like, but not exactly, rich versus poor. But it turns out the poor actually fight back,” he said.

Mr Vinokur has also published a dossier of evidence – “the Saks Files” – related to five other cases in which Saks’s employees alleged they were harassed, assaulted, or sexually assaulted and then fired or forced to leave.

It details lawsuits between 1994 and 2024. Most were settled out of court.

Mr Vinokur said the evidence suggested a “horrifying pattern”.

“I don’t want money. I want answers,” he wrote on his new website. “Saks pays women for confidentiality. I’m paying women to stand outside Saks Fifth Avenue every single day until they answer for this.”

A spokesman for Saks said: “We take matters of employee and customer safety and security extremely seriously.

“It is the company’s firmly held policy that we do not retaliate against any employee who reports violations of our policies or the law. All reports are investigated promptly and thoroughly.”

Mr Vinokur claimed that Saks’s legal team was pleading with him to stand his growing number of protesters down, but he has no such plans.

“That’s not my kind of personality. Like they f---ed with my mom,” he said.

“Saks need to be held accountable for this, and I’m going to make this law happen that’s going to protect all workers from being fired if they’re a victim of violent crime.”

Most states, New York included, do not have a law prohibiting termination because an employee was a crime victim. Only 25 states have mandated leave for employees who are victims of violent crimes.

Mr Vinokur said he had the time and money to continue the demonstration.

Come rain or shine, he said he would be outside Saks with his mother, other family members and the for-hire protesters. “What I was really touched by is the number of these women… who said: ‘When I read about this, it made me mad. That’s why I took this job’,” he said.

On Tuesday, Mr Vinokur extended the protests outside Bergdorf Goodman, Saks’s sister retailer. Next Monday, he said he had hired 90 protesters to disrupt Saks’s Christmas light show.

The department store sits across Fifth Avenue from the Rockefeller Centre Christmas tree – New York’s focus of festivities and a magnet for shoppers and visitors during peak holiday times.

Mr Vinokur said: “My audience is [the equivalent size of] Madison Square Garden Stadium every two hours. They are giving us the biggest stage in America and it’s free, no tickets.

“So I don’t want Saks to cancel the show. I want the stage.”

data.title: BT races to stop new Grand Theft Auto game crashing the internet
data.description:
BT is racing to prevent the latest instalment of Grand Theft Auto from crashing the internet as gamers rush to get a first taste of the hit title.

The telecoms giant is among the major broadband providers that have increased network capacity ahead of the rollout of the much-delayed GTA VI on Nov 19, which is expected to trigger “unprecedented” demand for data.

Several internet firms are understood to have bought more capacity from major exchanges including the London Internet Exchange (LINX) to handle the spike in traffic.

BT and other companies have also increased their use of caching – where data is temporarily stored in locations closer to the end user – limited scheduled maintenance and stepped up network monitoring.

The release of GTA VI, which is made by developer Rockstar Games, has already broken records for internet demand after fans were given a chance to pre-load the game a week ahead of its launch.

Virgin Media O2 reported its biggest-ever traffic peak and highest-ever daily data volume on Nov 10, with demand surging between midnight and 1am. LINX has recorded its highest ever traffic over the past month at 13.7 terabits per second (Tbps).

The pre-launch was also the second-biggest peak recorded across BT’s broadband network, behind only Arsenal’s Champions League semi-final clash against Atlético Madrid in May.

The eagerly-awaited release has sparked fears of congestion and disruption following similar issues during the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III in 2023.

While Rockstar has sought to limit the impact by spreading downloads of GTA VI over a week, experts warned this may not be enough to prevent disruption.

William Manzione, at network provider RETN said: “Pre-loading should help reduce the concentration of downloads on launch day, but it does not eliminate the possibility of further traffic increases.

“Players who have not preloaded the game may still download it on release day, while additional patches or updates could create another wave of demand.”

Mr Manzione said the most likely fallout would be slower downloads and localised congestion, rather than widespread outages.

Jeanie York, VMO2’s chief technology officer, said: “GTA VI has already broken broadband records before players have even entered the game, and we’re preparing for another busy day when it launches next week.

“Fans downloading in advance will spread some of that demand, but it’s too early to say whether launch day will set another record.”

A BT spokesman said: “We are building the UK’s digital backbone and connecting and protecting the country like no one else. Our networks are built to support moments of huge national demand like this.

“From the biggest gaming launches to major sporting and cultural events, BT is investing in the scale, capacity and resilience needed to keep millions of customers connected when it matters.”

GTA has been dogged by controversy since its first release in 1997 owing to the game’s graphic depiction of violence, as well as other themes including drugs, prostitution and sex.

But the game, which is largely developed by teams based in Scotland, has enjoyed runaway success. The last title in the series, GTA V, has generated more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in sales since its launch in 2013, making it the third-best-selling video game of all time.

Rockstar, which is owned by US games giant Take-Two Interactive, first unveiled plans for its sixth instalment in late 2023.

The title is rumoured to have a budget of up to $3bn, eclipsing any Hollywood movie, but has been beset by leaks and delays.

In August, Netflix agreed a deal for an exclusive early trailer of the gangland action game. The 25-minute clip racked up 31.1m views in its first four days, jumping to the top of the streaming service’s charts.

data.title: Labour’s ‘unfair’ bank tax will have consequences, warns JP Morgan boss
data.description:
The boss of JP Morgan has warned that John Healey’s bank tax raid will have consequences for Britain, as he vowed to set an “example” by finding ways to claw back the levy.

In a veiled threat to the Government, Jamie Dimon said he wanted politicians to “understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

Mr Dimon lashed out at the Chancellor after he temporarily doubled the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 6pc during his maiden Budget to provide “immediate support on energy bills”.

He said that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than in anger, but failed to specify how he would claw back the costs, as first reported by the Financial Times.

The Wall Street banking giant expects to pay between £100m to £150m because of Mr Healey’s higher surcharge.

Mr Dimon’s latest comments will renew scrutiny of JP Morgan’s proposals for a new £3bn headquarters in Canary Wharf.

The bank has not suggested any reversal to the tower’s development but it previously stressed that the project would depend on “a continuing positive business environment in the UK”.

The latest surcharge is levied in addition to the top rate of corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc.

That means the biggest banks in Britain now face a total tax rate of 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015.

Following the Budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated that the higher tax rate will bring in an extra £1.5bn for the Treasury.

However, it also claimed that the UK would lose roughly £190m of profits as a result of the tax rise.

Mr Dimon has been among the staunchest critics of the policy, with the bank previously claiming that it has paid £5.5bn in bank taxes since 2011.

In July, he said there would be “adverse consequences” if the Government targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes to help fund his spending plans.

“I always thought it was wrong,” he said. “We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.

“So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

JP Morgan declined to comment.

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.
