data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: Housebuilder shares slump as surging mortgage costs put off buyers
data.description:
Shares in one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders slumped after it warned that higher mortgage rates were putting off buyers.

Taylor Wimpey, which is listed on the FTSE 100, saw up to £130m wiped off its shares on Wednesday.

It now expects to sell 10,500 homes this year, down from July’s forecast of up to 10,800.

The group warned the housing market had been “challenging” during the autumn, with higher building costs combining with weaker house prices and rising interest rates for buyers.

This month, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years after warning inflation would rise close to 5pc in early 2027 as a result of the Iran war.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive of Taylor Wimpey, said: “The autumn selling season has been more subdued, as higher mortgage rates and living costs continue to reduce customer affordability.”

The housebuilder warned shareholders that it expected its adjusted operating profit to come in at the bottom of a range estimated by analysts at between £262m and £299m.

House prices rose at their slowest pace in nearly three years during October, according to a closely watched index from Nationwide.

Property values have been hit by higher mortgage rates, which have put strain on buyers.

The average five-year fixed deal with lenders stood at just under 6pc on Tuesday, up from just under 5pc on the eve of the Iran war outbreak, according to Moneyfacts.

In a further blow to the housing market, traders expect the Bank may raise interest rates again to 4.25pc in December.

Money markets suggest rates will rise to 4.75pc by July next year.

Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, said Taylor Wimpey had cut its sales forecasts as “higher mortgage rates continue to squeeze affordability”.

He added: “Pricing continues to reflect subdued market conditions.”

The company said it welcomed the Government’s Your First Home Scheme announced in the Budget last month.

The programme, expected to open for applications in February, aims to help first-time buyers purchase a new-build home with deposits as low as 2.5pc and a 20pc equity loan.

Ms Daly added: “We welcome the Government’s Your First Home Scheme to support getting people on to the property ladder.

“Our strong first-time buyer proposition and growing outlet base position us well as the scheme develops.”

Shares fell up to 5pc before recovering to be down 3pc.

data.title: Lime bike jousters defy warnings from company to stop
data.description:
“Joust, joust, joust,” the crowds jeered, as two knights charged towards one another, lances raised.

You might be forgiven for thinking the scene had been lifted from medieval Camelot.

But, atop a neon-green steed, the “knights” in question were taking part in a new phenomenon called “Lime bike jousting”, which sees riders on the rental e-bikes charge at one another brandishing striped poles.

Jack Carden, an artist, and actor Camtholomew the First, whose real name is Cameron Carnegie-Brown, staged their first duel earlier this month, drawing hundreds of spectators to London Fields, east London.

Footage of the first duel showed the pair charging towards one another on the e-bikes, dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and full suits of armour.

Each wielded a striped lance as they attempted to knock their opponent from his saddle.

But their medieval enthusiasm was not shared by Lime.

The company said in a statement: “While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first. Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.”

The company also discouraged riders from “attempting similar events”.

The men defied the warnings to stop and took part in another event on Saturday, called Lime bike Jousting 2: No Horses, No Mercy.

More than 5,000 people had registered their interest within a day of the invitation going online.

The organisers received police approval for the mass gathering and dropped the exact location coordinates just an hour and a half before the duel.

Hundreds of spectators descended on the park in an assortment of medieval finery and Hallowe’en fancy dress, transforming the east London park into a makeshift jousting arena.

Mr Carden said before the contest began: “This is a very special moment, not just for us, but for London... this is the most viewed joust of the modern era.”

The combatants were helped into their armour by their entourage before mounting their electric steeds, decorated for the occasion. “Ring maidens” in medieval dress set out the various rounds.

The pair battled through five rounds, with Mr Carnegie-Brown eventually claiming victory after landing the decisive blow.

Both Mr Carden and Mr Carnegie-Brown said that crowd safety was their “biggest priority” at the event. There were organising stewards to help with crowd control and health professionals on hand.

Hackney council said it did not give permission for the event to be held in the borough, but organisers claimed that they had informed the council that the event was going ahead with a full safety team.

The two “knights” competed in the duel for charity, raising more than £1,200.

The charities include The Bike Project, which fixes second-hand bikes and gives them to refugees, Honour Thy Woman Group, a domestic abuse charity, and the Mental Health Foundation.

There was even a seal of approval from the world of traditional jousting.

Andy Deane, the captain of the Royal Armouries jousting team in Leeds, said it was a “joy” to see the bike jousting “capturing the spectacle” of the medieval sport.

“This is absolutely a legitimate form of jousting,” he said following the first joust.

Mr Carden told The Telegraph: “We informed the council it was going ahead. We had a full safety team with first aiders, safety stewards, clean up crew, and had a chat with police before going ahead to ensure everything would be safe.

“We have been in touch with Lime from the first joust and they have at no point told us not to go ahead, merely to reinforce safety messages.”

Lime has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.

data.title: The world is facing a new credit crunch
data.description:
High above the streets of Los Angeles, residents of the Beaudry can gaze across the Hollywood skyline, take a dip in a heated saltwater pool, practise their swing on a golf simulator and even send their dog to the spa.

Living in the 64-storey skyscraper doesn’t come cheap. Its 785 apartments command average rents of $4,200 (£3,200) a month, and 95pc are occupied.

By most measures, the $600m building sounds like a property developer’s dream. So why did its owner choose to hand back the keys?

Brookfield, the Canadian asset management giant that built the tower, decided last month that walking away made more sense than refinancing the $360m loan attached to it.

The company said the decision reflected the “entrenched market challenges” facing a city where property values had failed to rebound as strongly as expected. The pandemic hit Los Angeles particularly hard. Office vacancy rates remain roughly double what they were before Covid struck.

But the Beaudry’s troubles offer a cautionary tale about a global financial system being tested to its limits.

The tower is one of the most high-profile casualties of what Larry Fink, the high priest of global finance and boss of BlackRock, has called “the biggest competition for capital I have seen in 50 years in finance”.

For almost two decades, money was cheap. In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the credit crunch it triggered, central banks around the world cut interest rates close to – or sometimes below – zero. Easy borrowing kept economies afloat.

But in recent years that reality has been shattered. Inflation has come roaring back after multiple energy shocks and wars, sending interest rates soaring. At the same time, governments have borrowed heavily to fund ballooning liabilities following the pandemic. Add into the pot AI companies spending historic sums, and you have a dangerous cocktail.

“Governments across the developed world are running huge deficits,” Fink warned last month. “That borrowing is now colliding with tremendous demand from the private sector, much of it from technology companies.”

Today, a new credit crunch is setting in. Unlike the global financial crisis, when lending markets effectively froze up, money is still available.

But there is a growing divide between those who can still borrow at affordable rates and those struggling to borrow at all.

The consequences are being felt far beyond financial markets. In Britain, Landsec, one of the country’s biggest property companies, has shelved a £1.5bn redevelopment of Lewisham Shopping Centre in south-east London that would have delivered more than 1,700 homes.

Meanwhile, British Land has paused the next phase of its vast Canada Water regeneration project in Rotherhithe, south London, which was originally expected to deliver 4,000 new homes.

These are far from isolated examples. Across London, at least 42,000 homes have effectively been priced out of the development pipeline, including 12,000 affordable properties, according to analysis by Savills.

Companies are cutting jobs as their debt interest bills rise, and some are teetering on the brink.

The drama is playing out in slow motion, spread over years as companies, households and governments come to refinance loans and face much higher costs than the rock-bottom rates they enjoyed.

We may be at the beginning of this financial squeeze. The question is, how bad could it become?

Debt clock is ticking

Nearly 5,500 miles away from the Beaudry, another debt drama is playing out in Britain.

After almost three years of financial limbo, a decision on the future of debt-laden Thames Water may finally be in sight.

Britain’s biggest utility, which serves 16 million customers, stumbled into crisis after running up debts of around £13bn by 2020. As interest rates have jumped, that debt pile has soared to around £20bn.

The company’s creditors are putting the finishing touches to a “last and final” rescue bid for the stricken utility, after a previous proposal was rejected by ministers in June.

The lenders – a consortium of more than 100 financial institutions from across the globe – hope to persuade a Prime Minister who has pledged greater public control of utilities to give his blessing to the deal.

But sources said time was running out.

Some creditors are increasingly reluctant to provide fresh capital for Thames to meet its day-to-day spending commitments while so much political and regulatory uncertainty hangs over deliberations.

Others are considering walking away altogether and putting their money to work in situations with far less risk, according to another person close to the negotiations. Pimco, the $2tn American bond behemoth, had to be persuaded to stay on board, sources said.

The challenge for financially stretched companies such as Thames is that lenders can increasingly find safer and more attractive opportunities elsewhere.

“There is an ever-growing, unprecedented level of debt financing requirements, so debt investors are asking themselves: ‘I can either put my money into the AI rollout or into water, offshore wind farms or other forms of infrastructure’,” a City source said.

It is an extraordinary choice. Investors are weighing up whether to finance the pipes delivering water to millions of British homes or the data centres powering the AI revolution.

Unlike Thames and other debt-laden utilities whose credit ratings have long languished deep in junk territory, companies such as Meta and Microsoft retain strong investment-grade credit ratings despite enormous spending on AI infrastructure.

The sums involved are staggering. America is on course to pour more than $10tn into AI between 2025 and the start of the next decade, according to the Brookings Institution, a think tank.

As a share of the economy, the outlay will dwarf even the railway and telecoms booms of the past.

Despite growing concerns about the sheer level of borrowing taking place to bankroll the AI race, “much of this debt is being issued by companies with low leverage and rising earnings, meaning they’re well-positioned to support that debt”, JP Morgan’s private banking arm said in a recent note to clients.

Alongside AI companies, governments are the other group borrowing as if there were no tomorrow. Institute for International Finance data show that since the pandemic, global public debt has climbed by $40tn to $110tn.

Governments ripped up their fiscal rulebooks and brought out their chequebooks to shield businesses and households from economic calamity.

Now, demographic pressures are also increasingly weighing on government spending. As Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England Governor, recently highlighted, public expectations of bailouts may not yet have “adjusted back” to pre-lockdown norms.

All of this is making life harder elsewhere.

JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, the longest-serving bank chief executive in America, has warned that soaring government borrowing costs and spending on the AI boom risk spilling over into the corporate debt markets, pushing up financing costs for companies everywhere.

“There will be a point where the market will ask for more and more and more, and at one point that’ll feed into corporate debt, corporate credit spreads and things like that,” Dimon said.

In a scramble to avoid a crunch, many companies have been “very aggressive” at reducing borrowings after interest rate rises following the pandemic and then Russia’s war in Ukraine, says Luke Reeve, the head of debt advisory at EY.

But thousands of companies face a day of reckoning. Companies around the world are sitting on a $26.4tn pile of debt, according to S&P Global Ratings, with $13tn needing to be refinanced in the next five years.

In Britain, close to £85bn of corporate debt is set to mature in 2027 alone, according to estimates from EY. Of that, £27.5bn is in the form of bank loans and £57.2bn is owed to the bond markets.

For most, this so-called “refinancing wall” will manifest itself as a sharp rise in borrowing costs.

Even those that moved early have paid a steep price. In 2024, Ocado partially refinanced £500m of debt and saw its interest rate jump from 3.9pc to 10.5pc. The online grocer has since laid off hundreds of staff as it grapples with pressure to cut costs.

For the weakest companies, however, the problem is not simply that borrowing has become more expensive.

It is that investors may refuse to lend altogether.

“Too many businesses have extended and pretended because of the cheap capital,” says Arif Husain, the chief investment officer and head of global fixed income at T Rowe Price.

“We’re going to see a lot more differentiation between good and bad businesses going forward.”

Pressure is already starting to show at the bottom of the market. Interest rates charged on “the worst of junk bonds” are the highest they have been for years, says Husain.

“For the worst companies, that is being reflected in their borrowing costs right now.”

Healthcare, technology and media are the most vulnerable sectors to debt crises, according to S&P.

The scale of the challenges is daunting; companies at greater risk of default have to roll over $61.2bn of debt in 2027, a figure set to rise to $222bn in 2028.

Will they be able to?

“Strong, cash-rich companies can still borrow easily, just at higher rates,” Stephanie von Friedeburg, a senior banker at Citi, told an audience at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok last month.

“But lower-rated and leveraged companies face a tough refinancing wave that will test their business model.”

A shake-out is already under way.

More than $5bn of debt deals were shelved across the US and Europe last month amid struggles to borrow, according to Bloomberg.

A total of seven companies pulled fundraising plans in October, the biggest spate of postponements this year.

These include AVI-SPL, a Florida-based software firm, which abandoned attempts to raise $690m, and Mesirow Financial, a Chicago-based wealth manager, which put a $175m bond sale on ice.

In Europe, German energy outfit Iqony pulled a €550m (£460m) debt refinancing at the start of November amid subdued investor appetite, just days after a loan intended to finance a €2bn private equity-led takeover of French beauty and wellness brand Aroma-Zone was scrapped.

The borrowers may be very different, but the message from investors is increasingly the same: they are no longer prepared to finance every deal at any price.

And as companies struggle to find willing lenders, another major source of global capital is beginning to retreat.

For decades, oil-rich Gulf states were among the world’s most enthusiastic financiers, pouring their petrodollars into everything from luxury London hotels to American technology giants.

Now, Gulf money is turning inwards. As the Iran war piles pressure on government finances, those same sovereign wealth funds that helped to bankroll Western companies and infrastructure projects are increasingly being called upon to support their own economies.

BlackRock estimates that up to $100bn of Gulf capital could be redirected towards domestic investment in the near term.

Mounting costs to build

As the great wave of credit that washed across the world retreats, things are starting to come undone.

As Warren Buffett said: “You don’t find out who’s been swimming naked until the tide goes out.”

In the UK, the clearest signs of stress can be found in the property market. For many developers in London, the sums no longer add up.

Roughly 96pc of new homes in London are flats. The cost of building them has climbed by 60pc in the past decade, but their value has risen by just 10pc, according to Savills.

Berkeley Group, one of the country’s biggest builders, has said building homes in London is becoming impossible.

This is largely because of rising costs and red tape. Recent analysis by the Centre for Policy Studies warned that government rules had added up to £442,000 to the cost of a London home.

But soaring borrowing costs play a part too. Unaffordable mortgages are hitting demand. Higher mortgage rates are squeezing buyers, particularly those considering flats, and leaving developers uncertain whether they can sell properties at prices that justify the cost of construction.

Beyond property, signs of stress are emerging elsewhere. Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) this month outlined plans to cut thousands of jobs as it grapples with an escalating debt crisis.

The telecoms group is seeking to strip out £800m of costs per year amid growing concerns about its ability to service a £22bn debt pile.

VMO2’s bonds have slumped as investors baulk at the outlook for the company, which is facing fierce competition from broadband start-ups and uncertainty about its ability to buy up smaller rivals.

A record 738,144 UK businesses were in “significant” financial distress at the end of August, according to restructuring company Begbies Traynor.

It said many were “operating with limited financial headroom”. The firm has been producing its Red Flag report, which looks at the health of UK Plc, since 2004.

Spreading the risks everywhere

Even as rising borrowing costs put pressure on businesses, the debt-fuelled AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.

In the past 12 months, AI companies have received almost two thirds of US venture-capital dollars.

A quarter of US investment-grade debt issued this year has come from companies involved in AI, according to Goldman Sachs.

Yet there are cracks emerging there too, as some investors, such as New York City’s $325bn pension system, start turning down AI deals amid concerns about overexposure.

“You’ve really got to be in every asset class, and we are in every major economy on Earth. But now so much of that, sector by sector, market by market, is AI,” Mark Levine, the New York City comptroller, told Semafor, the US news platform.

It’s “a risk that we’re leery of”, said the city’s equivalent of a chief finance officer.

Tremors have begun to appear in the market, with shares and bonds of “neocloud” data centre companies falling sharply in recent weeks.

Governments, too, have faced warning shots that investors will not tolerate their gorging on debt forever. Bond yields have hit multi-decade highs across the West in a sign of unease. The International Monetary Fund has told countries to rein in borrowing urgently to avert a crisis – before it’s too late.

Not everyone will lose out in this new credit squeeze.

Rich investors may find themselves in an increasingly powerful position as companies compete for their cash. Many of those with money looking for a home for it will be “licking their lips”, says Reeve at EY.

For most of us, however, the consequences of a prolonged period of expensive borrowing could be far less welcome. Homeowners will come under pressure, debt-laden companies will cut jobs and governments will surely have to scale back spending, reducing public services in the process.

“Clearly, the people that will suffer most will be the ones that need to borrow the most,” says Husain at T Rowe Price. “The bigger mortgages – [more] higher leveraged consumers – will be most at risk here.”

A new financial world order is emerging, where money is increasingly flowing towards the strongest borrowers and away from those who need it most.

In the face of this new credit squeeze, even a skyscraper full of paying tenants is struggling.

data.title: Buses to be driven by teenagers as operators face staff shortages
data.description:
Teenagers will be allowed to drive buses for school trips and weddings as part of a government shake-up to tackle shortages.

Ministers confirmed on Friday they were exploring changes to licensing rules that currently stop 18 and 19-year-olds from undertaking certain kinds of journeys.

Currently, they can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but operators can only assign them regular routes of less than 50 kilometres (31 miles).

The Department for Transport (DfT) wants to give teenagers the right to take on longer journeys and “non-regular” jobs as well, such as school trips, weddings, transport for football matches and holiday tours.

As well as tackling driver shortages, the DfT said the shake-up would provide more opportunities for young people at a time when around one million aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training – also known as Neets.

However, the Government said it was also considering potential safety issues with young drivers more prone to being in accidents than their elders.

It acknowledged that only limited data were available on young bus drivers, but pointed to wider road transport data showing that nearly a quarter of collisions resulting in deaths last year involved drivers aged 17 to 24.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for buses and local transport, said: “We want to clear the roadblocks that have been preventing too many young people from getting behind the wheel of a rewarding career.

“The proposed changes will help more 18 and 19-year-olds get into the bus and coach sector, giving them the opportunity to build skills, earn a living and develop a rewarding career, while maintaining the highest standards of road safety.”

This came after ministers separately lowered the minimum age for train drivers in Britain from 20 to 18 earlier this year amid a youth worklessness crisis.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has described the current number of jobless young people as an “economic catastrophe and moral failure”.

In consultation documents published on Friday, the DfT said there were an estimated 113,900 bus and coach drivers in the UK but only around 500 were aged 18 or 19.

Keith McNally, of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, which represents bus and coach operators, said the sector had also been battling a recruitment crisis since the Covid pandemic, which prompted some older drivers to retire while problems securing tests stopped new ones from qualifying.

“We’ve had shortages, so we think the opportunity to bring in more young people and let them experience what our industry has to offer is very positive,” he said.

The current rules “have some inconsistencies”, Mr McNally added, with teenage lorry-drivers not facing equivalent curbs.

At the moment, 18 and 19-year-olds can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but they are restricted to driving regular scheduled services of less than 31 miles.

This effectively means they can take on most local bus routes, school bus work and some inter-city services run by the likes of National Express and Flixbus.

However, it excludes them from school field-trips, football-team transport, weddings and other private-hire contracts.

Such non-regular services make up the majority of trips carried out by the coach sector, Mr McNally said.

He also sought to ease safety concerns by claiming that young drivers of buses and heavy goods vehicles are “just as safe as people who are older than them”.

“We don’t believe there are legitimate safety issues here, not least because of the training and selection processes that companies have got in place,” he said.

The Government’s consultation closes on Dec 18.

data.title: Major US banks go down for thousands of customers
data.description:
Thousands of bank customers across the US were unable to access their accounts on Monday as a number of major institutions suffered technical issues.

The banks affected included Bank of America, Chase, Wells Fargo and Capital One. Officials said the issue was a “technical” problem and not the result of a cyber attack.

It was not immediately clear what the technical problems were.

On Monday afternoon, United Airlines also reported a widespread system outage which delayed flight departures.

The airline said the issue was now fixed, but it affected flights for several hours. The service failure was not related to cybersecurity, United said.

The outages followed a meltdown on Friday when Microsoft users were unable to access their emails and other services.

That same day, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all passenger flights across the US after experiencing “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

It was only the second time since 9/11 that the FAA had ordered such a grounding, and more than 9,000 flights were cancelled. The White House said the issue was to do with ageing systems and was not the result of a cyber attack.

Microsoft said the two incidents were not related.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” said a spokesman for Chase on Monday. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly affected. However, it added that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays”.

Zelle is the payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family without having to use America’s slow and expensive wire services.

The system is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.

A spokesman for Early Warning Services said that the Zelle network was fully operational. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.

The problems ranged from issues accessing accounts, to problems with the banks’ apps. In many cases, things were simply slower than usual.

It was reported that some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

data.title: Fridges secured from hackers in secret operation
data.description:
Tens of thousands of fridges in Britain have been secured against hackers.

IT teams have been working for weeks to fix software issues that left fridges and freezers at supermarkets, restaurants and petrol stations vulnerable to cyber attacks.

Commercial fridges were shut off across Europe earlier this month, including at Swedish furniture chain Ikea and hundreds of grocery shops in France.

Large amounts of food were spoilt after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and raised their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Security researchers have found flaws in the cyber security of UK fridges and have warned supermarkets to take their devices offline while they fix them, it has been reported.

The secretive operation has not been reported until now to avoid hackers exploiting the vulnerability.

‘You’re in a race against time’

Ken Munroe, founder of PenTest Partners, part of the team combating the threat, told BBC Radio 4 that a weakness in passwords gave hackers an entry point into the systems.

He said: “Once they’ve [security flaws] been found, you’re in a race against time to make sure you can get them fixed before hackers use them.

“There were issues to do with weak credentials [in the Europe attacks] – once you knew how to make the passwords you can get in. There was something similar and related to these controls that we found was very popular in the UK.”

France’s blood bank was also hacked, while in the UK a handful of food suppliers have reported that their fridge units had their temperatures turned up to dangerous levels.

The hackers exploited weaknesses in the systems that connect industrial refrigerators to the internet, taking them over remotely and tampering with them.

Some cyber security researchers suggested the attacks bore the hallmarks of Russia. The Kremlin said it was “absurd” to suggest that Russian-backed hackers were behind the assault.

Two pro-Russian “hacktivist” groups, called NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest, took credit for the attacks in posts on the encrypted messaging app Telegram.

However, other experts cast doubt on the groups’ claims, arguing the hackers – who are also known as the Cyber Army of Russia Reborn – were typically responsible for more opportunistic attacks.

Last month’s hacks in France affected fridges supplied by Danish cooling giant Danfoss. Danfoss said the machines had been running outdated software. Danfoss is also a supplier to British chains including Tesco and Sainsbury’s.

In response to the hacks, Danfoss has claimed that most of the affected French fridges were either legacy systems or newer ones running on outdated software.

Water, sewage and power ‘vulnerable’

Mr Munroe said UK supermarkets now faced a “hugely reduced risk”. He said: “Who thought two months ago that fridges was going to be the next major attack for hackers?

“Even I didn’t see that one coming, and I’ve been working in this space for 30-plus years now. It’s all the other unrelated things – the systems we don’t think about, maybe the systems controlling our power supplies, maybe our water feeds, those things we don’t think about.”

Water, sewage and power supply systems are “40, 50, 60 years old”, Mr Munroe said, meaning they could be vulnerable to modern hacking technologies.

The National Cyber Security Centre is looking at other food and retail technologies that may be vulnerable to hacks, The Telegraph understands. Security agencies were believed to be in the process of contacting smaller businesses whose fridges may remain vulnerable.

Britain’s cyber security chiefs issued an alert to retailers earlier this month after European officials said the hacking of supermarket fridges had been a threat to food security.

Dozens of grocery shops in Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia were targeted at the end of October, causing at least €100,000 (£88,000) in food losses. One shop manager in Sweden said temperatures in his fridges had been turned up to 55C.

The Government has urged households to stockpile enough essential supplies to survive for three days amid the growing threat from emergencies such as cyber attacks.

Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said potential scenarios included power cuts or situations when “your local shop is subject to a cyber attack”. Technology disruptions have hit banks, airlines and businesses across the US in the past few weeks.

On Tuesday, 178 of the world’s biggest companies were hit in a cyber attack targeting users’ data, including credit card details. Zoom, CNN, the BBC, HSBC, IKEA, Fox News, and NPR were among the websites affected.

A major Microsoft outage last Thursday and Friday disrupted services including Outlook and Teams, affecting businesses and public services across more than 70 countries, including the UK.

data.title: Reverse NI tax raid or watch 40,000 jobs disappear, Burnham warned
data.description:
Tens of thousands of jobs in pubs, restaurants and hotels will be lost unless Andy Burnham reverses Labour’s jobs tax, hospitality bosses have warned.

UKHospitality, an industry trade body, urged the Prime Minister to back tax cuts that would benefit almost a quarter of a million jobs and help tackle Britain’s youth unemployment crisis.

The warning follows a landmark review by Alan Milburn, the former health secretary, who criticised the barrage of higher employment costs and regulations imposed on businesses.

Mr Milburn called on ministers to make it “cheaper and less risky” for businesses to hire young people, including by cutting employers’ National Insurance bills.

However, the proposals face resistance from the Treasury, despite sympathy from John Healey, the Chancellor, for efforts to tackle youth unemployment.

The trade body warned that another 40,000 hospitality jobs could disappear over the next year unless the Government reduces the cost of hiring workers.

More than 15,000 of those jobs are expected to be held by young people, worsening a crisis that has already left nearly a million 16 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet).

Mr Milburn proposed doubling the earnings threshold at which employers start paying the tax for workers aged 21 to 24 in hospitality, retail and leisure, from £5,000 to £10,000.

It would represent a partial reversal of Rachel Reeves’s £25bn raid announced in the former chancellor’s maiden Budget.

UKHospitality has estimated that the measure would benefit around 240,000 jobs in the sector and save businesses £170m a year.

Writing for The Telegraph, Allen Simpson, UKHospitality’s chief executive, warned that the Government risked condemning thousands more young people to unemployment unless it acted.

He said: “Let’s be clear, there is no Milburn review without the National Insurance cut it recommends. We will not get jobs for young people flowing without the high street and the high street won’t start hiring again without costs coming down.”

Mr Healey is said to be sympathetic to efforts to tackle youth unemployment, though Treasury officials are understood to be resisting plans to cut taxes for businesses hiring under-25s over concerns about the cost to the Exchequer.

However, Mr Simpson warned that refusing to act would cost the Treasury even more as young people are pushed on to benefits.

Nearly 100,000 hospitality jobs have already disappeared since Labour came to power, accounting for 45pc of all jobs lost across the economy during that period, according to the business group.

Mr Simpson said: “I would estimate, extrapolating the past two years of employment data, that we could see another 40,000 people lost from hospitality alone in the next 12 months unless we start to repair the damage. More than 15,000 of those, statistically, are likely to be young people.

“That’s more doomscrolling in bedrooms. More young people’s lives on hold and more benefits for the taxpayer to fund.”

He urged Downing Street to overrule Treasury objections and implement Mr Milburn’s recommendations.

Mr Simpson added: “This is a time for courage against intransigence. Downing Street need to face down the opponents of the review.”

It comes as Deutsche Bank warned that forecasts from the Milburn review that 440,000 more young people will be in work from his recommendations “may be slightly overstated”.

Economists at the bank said that rough calculations showed that the policies are more likely to move 200,000 young people into work by 2036.

They said that Britain’s weak labour market, health-related inactivity taking longer to solve than planned and the success rates of previous employment support schemes meant that the UK’s Neet rate is more likely to fall to 9pc by 2036, compared to 6.8pc estimated in the Milburn review.

The Treasury has been contacted for comment.

It simply costs too much to hire young workers

By Allen Simpson

The UK faces a Neets crisis. That much is obvious. The real question is: does the Government have the courage to make the tough decisions urged by Alan Milburn in his review this week?

Young people across the country have been left without a route into work, education or training. Left doomscrolling in their bedrooms, according to Milburn, without any real hope of building the lives previous generations have taken for granted.

The review was absolutely clear on what needs to be done. Yes, young people need better support. We spend a fraction of the money to help young people into work that we did 40 years ago.

And yes, there has to be a bit of stick with the carrot. If a young person doesn’t engage with the system, there should be consequences.

But Milburn was clear too that for much of the economy, the cost of employing a young person has simply become too high. We have priced employers out of business and young people out of work.

His solution was a targeted cut in National Insurance costs, only for hospitality and retail, and only for young people.

Unsurprisingly, that’s the bit it seems the Government is less keen on.

In 2024, Rachel Reeves used the first Labour Budget in 14 years to raise employer National Insurance contributions.

She did it by lowering the threshold at which pay starts to be taxable, which meant that the effect on lower earners – young people and people working part-time – was more than twice the effect on people earning six-figure salaries.

The result was immediate and crushing. In hospitality alone, around 100,000 jobs were lost. The same story in retail. The high street as a whole lost more jobs in two years than mining lost in the entirety of the 1980s.

It was an unprecedented attack on a single sector.

For 20 years, hospitality has been a rare protection against the Neets crisis becoming a disaster – creating jobs where other sectors were automating roles away.

But consecutive Budgets in 2024 and 2025 all but reversed that.

Three things need to be true for a young person to get a job. First, the businesses which actually employ them need to be viable. Second, the cost of hiring a young person needs to be affordable. And third, you need to be able to hire and develop them easily.

Today, all three are at risk.

Hospitality businesses pay 82pc of their profits in tax, which is higher than any other sector and twice the rate of banks. That figure has gone up significantly in recent years.

The cost of employing a 21-year-old is now 77pc higher than before the pandemic.

And the Employment Rights Act has made employers nervous of taking a risk on people without a track record.

Milburn’s solution of a targeted reversal of the National Insurance increase is modest against the scale of the problem, especially if introduced gradually over five years.

It will be a fraction of the tax grab of the past two years and easily recouped from higher tax receipts and lower benefits by moving young people back into work.

But the word from the Treasury has been that they oppose even this small step towards making first jobs viable.

White smoke in the press and to businesses has been that they are just not willing to make the investment needed to deliver job opportunities and a reduced benefits bill.

But let’s be clear, there is no Milburn review without the National Insurance cut it recommends. We will not get jobs for young people flowing without the high street and the high street won’t start hiring again without costs coming down.

I would estimate, extrapolating the past two years of employment data, that we could see another 40,000 people lost from hospitality alone in the next 12 months unless we start to repair the damage. More than 15,000 of those, statistically, are likely to be young people.

That’s more doomscrolling in bedrooms. More young people’s lives on hold and more benefits for the taxpayer to fund.

I know that the Prime Minister does not see the world this way and I’m not convinced the Chancellor does either.

This looks from the outside like a classic case of Treasury brain, where officials are more comfortable weighing the direct receipts of a tax than calculating the negative impacts, or indeed the positive ones from a cut.

It is the same mentality which led to them taxing away jobs in the first place.

This is a time for courage against intransigence. Downing Street needs to face down the opponents of the review.

Milburn was asked a question by the Government and he gave the right answer. It needs to be implemented without delay.

Allen Simpson is the chief executive of UKHospitality

data.title: Channel 4 chief: Handling of Russell Brand complaints ‘almost unforgivable’
data.description:
Channel 4’s handling of complaints about Russell Brand was “almost unforgivable”, its chief executive has said.

Addressing MPs on Tuesday, Priya Dogra apologised to one of Brand’s victims who complained to the broadcaster about his behaviour in both 2009 and 2023.

In a victim statement read out in court ahead of Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault on Nov 5, the woman, who was referred to as Bella in The Times’s investigation, said her complaint had been “brushed under the carpet” by Channel 4 bosses.

Ms Dogra told the digital, media, culture and sport select committee on Tuesday that she was “horrified” to learn that other people had made complaints they felt were not dealt with properly.

She said: “That is not acceptable. It shouldn’t be. And in the instance of Bella, I’m not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice.”

The Channel 4 boss added: “I want to express my dismay and frustration that we end up in these cycles as a media industry. This is not what we want to be known [for] as an industry.”

Brand, who has begun a decade-long prison sentence, was convicted of sexually assaulting Bella in 2009 by demanding a massage and placing his head in her groin without her consent.

Bella, who has lifelong anonymity, reported the incident to Channel 4 the day after it happened but no action was taken.

Following the release of its Dispatches investigation into Brand in 2023, the broadcaster commissioned an internal inquiry into the disgraced comedian, who worked on programmes including Big Brother.

Alex Mahon, Channel 4’s chief executive at the time, apologised to Bella for failing to investigate her complaint.

But the former employee described the company’s inquiry as “shambolic” and described its report as a “whitewash”.

Ms Dogra said Channel 4 would not open another investigation into its handling of complaints, but insisted the broadcaster had strengthened its protections for staff.

She said the company had expanded its anonymous whistleblowing service, while it will now require all production companies it partners with to sign up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA), an industry-funded body aimed at cracking down on misconduct.

Geoff Cooper, Channel 4’s chairman, added that a change in culture was now a priority for the broadcaster’s board.

It comes after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, summoned TV bosses on Monday to call for an end to the culture of abuse across the media industry.

She has threatened to introduce tougher regulation if bosses fail to protect people from workplace abusers.

Ms Dogra acknowledged that the industry had a problem with power imbalances between stars and crew and said broadcasters would have to prove that commercial interests did not override their principles.

The Channel 4 boss pointed to her decision to axe Married at First Sight, which she described as a “very profitable show”, following allegations of rape on the reality show.

Ms Dogra, who took up the role in March, also defended Channel 4 and news producer ITN against criticisms about the widespread use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to silence former employees.

She said: “We do have clauses, but they are not intended to be gagging orders in any way. If somebody has seen misconduct or misbehaviour, they are open to report that.”

The Commons committee will grill TV bosses next month about whether NDAs are preventing people from reporting abuse and inappropriate behaviour in the media and entertainment industries.
